channel.title: The Brief — Adam's News
channel.description: Every story from Adam's three daily briefs (9 AM / 5 PM / 10 PM CT) as its own item, readable right in your feed reader, with a link to the original article.

item.title: Komyshuvakha toll still disputed, daytime drones continue, and a nuclear-plant employee is reported killed
item.description:
The confirmed death toll from Monday's strike on the humanitarian aid centre in Komyshuvakha, in the Zaporizhzhia region, still has not settled into a single figure on Tuesday evening — and that disagreement itself is the story. The evening brief put it at 31 dead with more than 45 missing, citing the regional administration. The BBC's later reporting, relayed Tuesday evening, put the confirmed toll at 33, with President Volodymyr Zelensky warning that more than 50 people could still be trapped under the rubble. An earlier BBC/TBS account from Tuesday morning had it at 26, including two emergency rescuers and four police officers, with 27 then reported missing. Rescue work has repeatedly been interrupted by the threat of further Russian drone attacks, according to the regional head, Mykhailo Semikin. Treat any single number tonight as provisional: the counts are moving as rubble is cleared, not because the facts are settled.
The two sides' accounts of what was hit have not moved closer. Zelensky says residents had gathered at a school building used weekly to distribute humanitarian aid, that Russian forces struck the school and then struck again where people had taken shelter, and that "the Russians could not have been unaware" civilians gathered there weekly. Russia's defence ministry, by contrast, said the attack targeted Ukrainian military units and killed 25 servicemen — a claim the BBC reported it found no credible evidence for, noting no major military or industrial facilities in the settlement. The same wave also hit a hospice in Dnipro and a hospital in Kharkiv, where Zelensky said 73 people were wounded, most of them elderly patients.
The fighting did not stop during the day. Ukraine's air force said Russia launched another 81 drones during Tuesday daytime, including 74 jet-powered models, of which defenders shot down or suppressed 62 — figures separate from the overnight barrage of 289 drones and 76 missiles covered in the earlier briefs. Separately, Reuters reported Tuesday that the management of the Russian-held Zaporizhzhia nuclear power plant said a Ukrainian drone killed two people in a car, including a female station employee — the third plant employee killed in the past two weeks and the 13th since April, according to the plant. Ukraine did not comment. The plant, Europe's largest with six reactors, is offline, and the UN nuclear watchdog's director general, Rafael Grossi, has repeatedly called for military restraint around it. The plant's statement gave no indication of where the incident occurred, so the location — and whether it was near the plant itself — is unconfirmed.
For ordinary Ukrainians, the practical picture heading into Wednesday is unchanged from the evening brief and still grim: emergency outages in seven regions, Kyiv water cuts, and three DTEK thermal plants halted. Diplomatically, the next marker is Wednesday, November 4, when Zelensky said teams from Ukraine, the US, Europe and NATO countries meet in Brussels to discuss recovery packages and security guarantees, ahead of the US-brokered Abu Dhabi talks on November 10–11 that Moscow has confirmed it will attend.
In short: the Komyshuvakha toll is still disputed — 31, 33, or higher once the rubble is cleared — daytime drone attacks continued, a Zaporizhzhia plant employee is reported killed in a drone strike Ukraine has not commented on, and the next diplomatic step is Wednesday's Brussels meeting, not yet a ceasefire.
Sources:
Source: augerton.com.

item.title: Saudi–Houthi: a disputed drone over Mecca, rival claims over the south-west, and a fresh US travel warning
item.description:
Tuesday's Saudi–Houthi exchange is a case study in two competing versions of the same day, with no independent confirmation of either side's full account. The Saudi-led coalition said it intercepted and destroyed a drone over the Mecca region on Tuesday, with coalition spokesman Maj. Gen. Turki al-Malki quoted by the Saudi Press Agency at 12:36 PM local time, and later said two more drones were destroyed — one over the Eastern Province, one heading south — bringing Tuesday's claimed total to three, according to Xinhua's relay. The Houthis rejected the Mecca claim outright: military spokesman Yahya Saree called it a "slanderous and recycled lie," AFP reported, and the movement has systematically denied targeting Islam's holy sites, a point it has made repeatedly in response to earlier Saudi claims about Mecca and Medina.
At the same time, the Houthis made their own claims that could not be independently verified: Saree said the group targeted Abha International Airport with a drone and King Khalid Air Base in Khamis Mushait with a ballistic missile, both in the south-western Asir region. And in the other direction, the Houthis said Saudi-led airstrikes killed 17 civilians over two days, most of them children, hitting residential areas and markets — a claim from Houthi-controlled health authorities that Saudi Arabia has not addressed in the reporting seen. Saree also said Riyadh carried out 109 strikes over the past 24 hours across Saada, Taiz, Lahj, Al-Jawf and Hodeidah. None of these casualty or strike counts is independently verified.
What is on the record from a third party is the US warning. The US Mission to Saudi Arabia updated its security alert on November 3, warning that Houthi attacks have hit civilian airports and critical infrastructure, causing casualties and severe travel disruption, and that hostilities could escalate rapidly beyond the immediate area. US government personnel now need special authorisation to travel to Qatif, Yanbu, Jizan, Asir, Najran and Taif, and may not go within 20 miles of the Yemen border. The alert itself describes no new strike — it is a warning, not a report of one — and it notes Riyadh airport has partially reopened while Jeddah and Dammam face delays and cancellations. That sits alongside the evening brief's report of Houthi ground raids across the south-western border and the Asian Cup postponement to late 2027: the pattern is a war widening from missiles and drones into border raids, event cancellations, and travel restrictions, even on days when the two sides cannot agree on what actually happened.
In short: the coalition claims three drone interceptions including one over Mecca, the Houthis deny the Mecca claim and claim their own strikes in the south-west while reporting 17 civilian deaths from Saudi strikes — none of it independently verified — and the US has tightened its own travel rules for the oil heartland and the Yemen border region.
Sources:
Source: lifenewsagency.com.

item.title: Iran: no new confirmed strike Tuesday evening; the Qeshm account stands as reported, not on the record
item.description:
The limited US strikes on Qeshm Island reported Monday by the Wall Street Journal — described by US officials to the Journal, AP and CNN as defensive strikes after Iranian surface-to-air fire at a US jet and an Iranian missile aimed at commercial shipping — still have no formal CENTCOM statement and no formal Iranian confirmation of a US attack, as of Tuesday evening.
Iran's position, reported Tuesday, remains that a deal is "far off" and Tehran will not accept "excessive demands," while Qatari mediators were due in Tehran on Tuesday night. Oil gave back part of Monday's sharp fall on Tuesday after the strike news broke.
Nothing Tuesday evening changes that picture; treat any new strike claim without an official statement as unverified. Sources:
Source: themedialine.org.

item.title: Poland: no new court move Tuesday evening, but Tusk offers private talks with Nawrocki
item.description:
Prime Minister Donald Tusk said Tuesday, after a National Security Council meeting, that he had offered to meet President Karol Nawrocki privately this week to ease tensions over the Constitutional Tribunal, keeping the timing private so they could speak candidly.
Nawrocki opened the council meeting by calling the suspensions of the tribunal's president and deputy unlawful and blaming Tusk for the police presence outside the court; Tusk called those remarks unnecessarily confrontational. The council also showed broad agreement on expanding the US military presence in Poland and establishing American bases, Tusk said.
This does not resolve Tuesday's split assembly — eight judges meeting and claiming a quorum, seven staying away — covered in the evening brief. Source:
Source: polandinsight.com.

item.title: Apple — iOS 27.3 beta arrives a day early, with Apple Intelligence in China:
item.description:
Apple released the first iOS 27.3 developer beta on November 3, and developers in China can now turn on Apple Intelligence, with Alibaba's Qwen powering some features, according to a November 3 AI-news roundup.
This is a developer beta, not a public launch, and it is the China availability that is new — not a new device. Treat the Qwen detail as reported in that roundup, not yet confirmed by Apple in the coverage seen.
Source:
Source: thediaryofai.com.

item.title: Polyend Tracker — Community Edition 1.0 open-sources the firmware:
item.description:
Polyend launched the firmware source code for its Tracker, Tracker+ and Tracker Mini music hardware on GitHub, alongside a Community Edition 1.0 model that lets users customise the firmware, build a new one, and distribute it — with new synths, sample streaming and plugins.
For musicians who own the hardware, this is the genuinely useful kind of open-source release: it turns a closed instrument into something the community can keep improving. Source:
Source: opensourceforu.com.

item.title: paperclipai/paperclip — manage AI agent teams like a company:
item.description:
An AI agent orchestration platform that places agents in an org chart and assigns them goals and budgets, trending on November 3 with +2,844 stars in 7 days and a latest release v2026.1023.0 from October 24.
It is a management layer for the agent boom rather than a new model — useful if you are already running many agents, less so if you are not. Source:
Source: trend.ondo.sh.

item.title: CodeQL 2.27.3 — Python 3.15 support and JSON data extensions:
item.description:

It rolls out automatically to GitHub code scanning users and will be in GitHub Enterprise Server 3.24. Source:

item.title: Chainstack breach disclosed November 3 — customer data and password hashes accessed:
item.description:
Blockchain infrastructure provider Chainstack said an attacker entered a development environment through a third-party component on October 26, reached production on October 29, was detected and cut off on October 31, and the incident closed November 2.
The attacker accessed a database with organisation names, account-holder names, member email addresses and password hashes, and had access to systems holding node credentials — which Chainstack says it has no evidence were read but is treating as exposed. Customers are being asked to rotate node credentials and regenerate API keys.
The company says services kept running normally and it does not store full payment-card details. Source:
Source: abijita.com.

item.title: MoneySmart breach (Singapore/Hong Kong) and SIA via Amadeus — both disclosed November 3:
item.description:
MoneySmart said an unauthorised party accessed internal IT systems on October 29 and copied some customer data, potentially including names, ID numbers, contact details, income ranges and shipping addresses.
Separately, Singapore Airlines said about 46,000 booking records were accessed via a breach at its reservation technology provider Amadeus, and that its own systems were not breached. Both are company disclosures, not yet independently audited for scope.
Source:
Source: cvetodo.com.

If you run PAN-OS with a management interface reachable from the internet, that is the configuration to check first. Source:

item.title: Russell Brand — no verdict Tuesday; jury sent home at 4 PM, back Wednesday:
item.description:
The jury at Southwark Crown Court began deliberating Tuesday just before 14:50 GMT after Judge Joel Bennathan finished summing up, and was sent home at 4 PM local time with no verdict, Reuters reports.
Deliberations resume Wednesday morning. Brand denies three counts of rape, three counts of sexual assault and one count of attempted indecent assault, involving six women over 1999–2009.
Nothing here is a finding of guilt. Separately, a New York judge on November 3 cleared a civil suit — an anonymous extra's sexual-assault claim against Brand and Warner Bros. from the 2010 shoot of *Arthur* — to proceed toward trial, denying the corporate defendants' motion to dismiss.
That civil ruling is not a verdict either. Sources:
Source: reuters.com.

item.title: Israel — opposition formally lines up behind Eisenkot, Shas behind Netanyahu; Herzog decides from Wednesday:
item.description:
Five opposition leaders met in Herzliya on Tuesday — Eisenkot, former prime minister Naftali Bennett, Avigdor Liberman, Yair Golan and Yair Lapid — and agreed all their parties will recommend Gadi Eisenkot to President Isaac Herzog, with negotiating teams drafting policy guidelines and coalition agreements immediately, according to The Media Line and Crisis.Zone.
The opposition holds 48 seats, Netanyahu's bloc 53, the Arab-led parties 19, with 61 needed — and the leaders have not settled whether to rely on Arab parties, which Liberman opposes. Shas, as reported in the evening brief, will recommend Netanyahu.
Herzog's consultations open Wednesday, starting with smaller parties, with Likud last on Thursday evening; the nominee then gets 28 days, extendable by 14. Sources:
Source: themedialine.org.

item.title: Ukraine update: aid-centre toll rises to 31 as outages and water cuts spread
item.description:
The death toll from Monday's strike on the humanitarian aid centre and shelter in Komyshuvakha, in the Zaporizhzhia region, has risen to 31, with more than 45 people still missing, according to the New York Post's wire report. Rescuers were still searching the cratered site on Tuesday. The overnight barrage itself — 289 drones, 17 ballistic missiles and 59 cruise missiles, as President Volodymyr Zelensky reported — is the same wave covered in this morning's brief; what changed during the day is the scale of the civilian fallout now being counted.
Ukraine's national energy company said Russia attacked its energy facilities more than 20 times, forcing emergency power outages in seven regions including Kyiv, and scheduled cuts elsewhere left some consumers without electricity for more than 12 hours — the first such outages this autumn, according to Ukrainska Pravda via the Post. Energy Minister Denys Shmyhal said Russia also hit a substation critical to the Khmelnytskyi Nuclear Power Plant, calling it a threat to the nuclear safety of all of Europe and saying he had spoken to the International Atomic Energy Agency. Major water supply facilities left without power interrupted Kyiv's water supply. DTEK, Ukraine's largest private generator, called it one of the most serious attacks ever on its facilities, with three of its five thermal plants halted. The UN Secretary-General condemned the continuing attacks on population centres, including strikes on a medical facility and a hospice in Kharkiv and Dnipro, and noted the record civilian casualties.
Diplomatically, the day moved in two directions at once. Zelensky travelled to Germany for talks with European leaders ahead of next week's US-brokered talks, and Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov confirmed on Tuesday that a Russian delegation will attend the Abu Dhabi talks on November 10–11 — the first such talks since February. No ceasefire or de-escalation was announced by either side.
Sources:
Source: nypost.com.

item.title: Iran update: "no rush" from Trump, "far from a deal" from Tehran — while the Qeshm strike stays unconfirmed on the record
item.description:
No government has put the Qeshm Island strike on the record. As of Tuesday afternoon US time, multiple US officials had told CNN, AP, the BBC/CBS and others that the US carried out limited "defensive" strikes on Qeshm on Monday after Iranian surface-to-air fire against US aircraft or assets, targeting radar and missile launchers — the Wall Street Journal first reported the operation — but US Central Command had issued no formal public statement and Iranian authorities had not formally confirmed a US attack on the island, according to NewsCubby's Tuesday update and The Media Line. IRNA reported several explosions on Qeshm on Monday night.
The two sides' public lines pulled in opposite directions on Tuesday. Trump told Axios on Monday there is "no rush" to decide on new strikes — "one way or the other, we will do something" — and told NBC News he was not considering striking Iran after the midterms, while also again raising Pickaxe Mountain, the suspected underground nuclear site, as a target. A senior Iranian official told Reuters the two sides are far from a deal and that Tehran will not accept Washington's "excessive demands," and parliamentary speaker Mohammad Bagher Qalibaf said Iran had given the US a "strong and rational response" and that "the ball is in the US' court." Qatari mediators were due in Tehran on Tuesday night to meet Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, according to Reuters via The Media Line. Oil, which fell sharply on Monday — Brent down 7.6% to $104.77, its biggest one-day drop since July — gave back part of that fall on Tuesday after the strike news broke.
Sources:
Source: newscubby.com.
item.content:encoded:
No government has put the Qeshm Island strike on the record. As of Tuesday afternoon US time, multiple US officials had told CNN, AP, the BBC/CBS and others that the US carried out limited "defensive" strikes on Qeshm on Monday after Iranian surface-to-air fire against US aircraft or assets, targeting radar and missile launchers — the Wall Street Journal first reported the operation — but US Central Command had issued no formal public statement and Iranian authorities had not formally confirmed a US attack on the island, according to NewsCubby's Tuesday update and The Media Line. item.title: Saudi–Houthi: reported cross-border ground raids, and the Asian Cup postponed
item.description:
A new report says the Houthi war has crossed a line beyond missiles and drones. Middle East Eye, citing a Western and an Arab official with direct knowledge, reports that Houthi fighters have launched multiple small-scale cross-border ground raids into Saudi Arabia's mountainous southwest in recent months, targeting border posts, with at least one raid as recently as the end of October — and that the raiders appear to have captured small arms and surveillance equipment used only by Saudi border forces. That account is relayed by OilPrice/ZeroHedge and has not been confirmed by Riyadh or the Houthis, so treat the scale as reported, not established. Separately, Bloomberg reports that the Asian Football Confederation has postponed its flagship tournament in Saudi Arabia until late 2027, citing "exceptional circumstances arising from developments in the region" — the latest major event to slip as Houthi attacks continue. On the diplomatic side, Saudi Defence Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman discussed de-escalation efforts with US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth by phone on Monday, and the coalition said it intercepted two drones targeting the Riyadh region on Monday night.
Sources:
Source: oilprice.com.

item.title: Israel update: Shas backs Netanyahu as Herzog's consultations open Wednesday
item.description:
The opposition's Eisenkot plan, covered in full this morning, gained a counterweight on Tuesday: the ultra-Orthodox Shas party said it will recommend Benjamin Netanyahu to President Isaac Herzog, citing his commitment to regulating the status of Torah students, according to Yedioth Ahronoth via The Insight International. Herzog begins consultations with parliamentary factions on Wednesday — starting with the smaller parties, with Likud last on Thursday evening — and the Central Elections Committee is expected to announce final official results on Wednesday. The new Knesset is sworn in on November 10. Nothing in Tuesday's announcements changes the arithmetic from this morning: Netanyahu's bloc 53, the Jewish opposition 48, the Arab-led parties 19, with 61 needed. KAN also reported on Monday that Eisenkot has ruled out serving in a Netanyahu-led government.
Sources:
Source: theinsightinternational.com.

item.title: Google — Guided Learning reaches Classroom, and school AI goes opt-in:
item.description:
Google announced on November 3 that Guided Learning — the Gemini mode that coaches students through a problem rather than handing them the answer — is now globally available in Google Classroom, with a pilot in Search at select US schools later in November.
The bigger policy change: Gemini, Gemini Notebook, Gemini in Classroom and Google Search will be entirely off for K-12 student accounts until a school administrator explicitly turns them on. The catch, flagged by 9to5Google and the New York Times: because Search and AI are "deeply integrated," schools that keep AI off also lose Search for their students, with two options promised for early 2027 — AI features on, or Guided Learning in their place.
Sources:
Source: blog.google.

item.title: CISA KEV — WordPress core added Tuesday:
item.description:
CISA updated its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on Tuesday afternoon for the first time since Friday, to version 2026.11.03 with 1,767 entries.
The one new entry is WordPress core CVE-2026-119977 — a flaw in the core update process where a staged copy of WordPress under wp-content/upgrade/ could be reached by an unauthenticated attacker during an upgrade window. Wordfence rates it 8.1; the fix is WordPress 7.1.4 or the matching backport.
Federal agencies have until Friday, November 6. Source:
Source: carthageelectronics.com.

item.title: Poland's top court splits in two — eight judges meet, seven stay away, and both sides claim the law
item.description:
Poland's Constitutional Tribunal held its disputed general assembly on Tuesday, and the result was two courts claiming to be one. Eight judges, all elected by the current Sejm, met in Warsaw under Judge Anna Korwin-Piotrowska, who suspended the tribunal's president and deputy on October 30. They ruled that they formed a quorum by counting 12 eligible judges — leaving out the suspended president Bogdan Święczkowski and deputy Bartłomiej Sochański, plus Judge Jarosław Wyrembak, whose election Korwin-Piotrowska called defective — and then adopted the tribunal's draft 2027 budget and drew lots for the disciplinary panels that will hear the cases of Święczkowski and Sochański. That is what RMF24 and Notes from Poland reported, via Crisis.Zone's live tracker. The other seven judges, including Święczkowski, stayed away; he dismissed the meeting as a "social gathering," and constitutional law expert Ryszard Piotrowski called it illegal.
The details behind the quorum fight matter because the whole crisis turns on a counting question. The tribunal has 15 seats, and a general assembly normally needs 10 judges present. Only eight judges elected by the current Sejm exist, so a 10-of-15 quorum was impossible without the other camp — which is why the eight redefined the denominator to 12. The budget vote was the practical trigger: without an approved revenue-and-expenditure plan, the tribunal's funds were not in next year's draft budget, and two earlier attempts to hold the assembly failed for lack of quorum, according to Interia's report of the meeting. Justice Minister Waldemar Żurek told Dziennik Gazeta Prawna that his immunity-lifting motions do not need a quorum, though adopting the budget does — and on Tuesday he filed a sixth motion to lift Święczkowski's immunity. Prosecutors separately opened an investigation into the alleged assault on judges Korwin-Piotrowska and Krystian Markiewicz at the building's entrance during President Karol Nawrocki's entry on October 31.
Each side's legal argument is now on the record, and neither has been tested before a body both accept. The government-backed judges say the Sejm's power to elect judges is constitutional, that the suspended leadership blocked the court from functioning, and that the European Commission and the Venice Commission back parliament's appointment power — the Commission said on Saturday that appointing the eight new members lies within the Sejm's constitutional power. The other camp, backed by the Supreme Court's College, says a suspension from duties does not end the president's term or create a vacancy, so Korwin-Piotrowska cannot lawfully direct the court; the College adopted a resolution on Tuesday saying the move to suspend the president and vice-president lacked a legal basis, with all 55 judges present backing it, according to PolandInsight. Nawrocki's camp calls the whole episode a forcible takeover — the tribunal's X account has used the word "coup" — while Prime Minister Donald Tusk has said restoring the rule of law is a duty and that there can be no compromise. The Supreme Court's own general assembly on Tuesday fell short of the quorum needed to adopt a resolution, leaving the College's statement as the judiciary's main counterweight.
For ordinary Poles, the immediate stakes are less abstract than the quorum maths. A paralysed constitutional court cannot rule on the laws parliament passes, the budget process for the court itself was the tripwire, and the standoff is already spilling into the street and the currency market: riot police were deployed at the court on Friday, protesters have gathered outside it for days, and Commerzbank noted on Tuesday that the institutional conflict is weighing on the zloty, with EUR/PLN briefly reaching 4.4372. With a general election a year away, both camps are also fighting over who gets to define the crisis — restoration of the rule of law, or a coup against a constitutional body.
In short: eight judges met, called themselves a quorum by counting 12 instead of 15, passed the 2027 budget and set disciplinary panels in motion against the suspended president and deputy — while the other seven judges stayed away, the Supreme Court's College said the suspensions had no legal basis, prosecutors opened an assault investigation, and the question of who lawfully runs Poland's top court remains unanswered by any body both sides accept.
Sources:
Source: crisis.zone.

item.title: Russia's election-day barrage hits Ukraine's power grid as the aid-centre toll rises to 29
item.description:
Russia launched a sweeping overnight bombardment of Ukraine's energy infrastructure on Tuesday, hours after the death toll from Monday's strike on a humanitarian aid centre in Zaporizhzhia rose to 29, with 48 people still missing. The barrage — 289 attack drones, 17 ballistic missiles and 59 cruise missiles across nine regions, according to President Volodymyr Zelensky — triggered emergency power cuts across the country and landed on the day of the US midterm elections, a timing Zelensky pointedly flagged.
The details, as reported by the Associated Press and Reuters, show a two-front night. In Komyshuvakha, the Zaporizhzhia village hit Monday, rescuers kept pulling bodies from the cratered aid facility and shelter through Tuesday, with acting regional military chief Mykhailo Semikin calling it "one of the worst tragedies in terms of the number of civilian victims in our region since the start of the full-scale war." The region declared three days of mourning. In the overnight wave, a strike on a city clinical hospital in Kharkiv wounded at least 62 people by local authorities' count — Zelensky put the hospital toll at 73 — and forced the transfer of more than 200 patients; in Dnipro, one person was killed and 17 wounded, with a woman pulled alive from rubble Tuesday morning. Ukraine's largest private generator, DTEK, said three of its five thermal power plants were knocked offline, and railways were hit as well. Russia's Defence Ministry said it carried out a "massive strike" on electricity facilities supplying military factories and on port infrastructure in Odesa. In the other direction, Ukraine's drones set fire to a major oil refinery in Yaroslavl, wounding two employees, according to the regional governor; Moscow's mayor said 493 drones were fired toward the capital, and Moscow-installed officials in Crimea imposed rolling blackouts after energy attacks there.
The two sides read the night in opposite ways. Zelensky framed the timing as a message to Washington: "The Russians think America won't notice this signal of theirs," he said, urging the US to "help Ukraine defend its skies; otherwise, Russia will never stop its missile strikes." Moscow's account is purely military: its Defence Ministry described strikes on facilities supplying Ukraine's army and arms factories, with no comment on the Komyshuvakha aid centre or the Kharkiv hospital. The gap between those accounts is the story — one side presenting a deliberate signal to an election-day America, the other presenting routine strikes on war infrastructure.
For ordinary people, the impact is heat, light and hospital beds. Emergency and unscheduled outages spread from Odesa in the south to Rivne in the west, three DTEK plants are offline, and hospital patients in two cities were moved mid-treatment. The Komyshuvakha search continues under the threat of further strikes, with dozens of families still waiting to learn whether the missing are alive. The diplomatic calendar adds pressure: US envoy Steve Witkoff has said Washington will mediate working-level talks between Ukrainian and Russian delegations in Abu Dhabi on November 10–11, a week after a night like this one.
In short: at least 29 dead and 48 missing from Monday's aid-centre strike, a 365-weapon overnight barrage that knocked out power plants and hit hospitals, Kyiv reading it as an election-day signal to Washington, Moscow calling it strikes on military supply — and Abu Dhabi talks a week away.
Sources:
Source: npr.brightspotcdn.com.

Emergency and unscheduled outages spread from Odesa in the south to Rivne in the west, three DTEK plants are offline, and hospital patients in two cities were moved mid-treatment. The Komyshuvakha search continues under the threat of further strikes, with dozens of families still waiting to learn whether the missing are alive. The diplomatic calendar adds pressure: US envoy Steve Witkoff has said Washington will mediate working-level talks between Ukrainian and Russian delegations in Abu Dhabi on November 10–11, a week after a night like this one.

In short: at least 29 dead and 48 missing from Monday's aid-centre strike, a 365-weapon overnight barrage that knocked out power plants and hit hospitals, Kyiv reading it as an election-day signal to Washington, Moscow calling it strikes on military supply — and Abu Dhabi talks a week away.

item.title: US strikes on Iran's Qeshm Island land on the eve of the midterms — while Doha mediators report progress
item.description:
The United States carried out limited strikes on Iran's Qeshm Island on Monday, the Wall Street Journal first reported, citing US officials — and three US officials confirmed the operation to CNN, describing it as defensive. The strike, on an island at the western end of the Strait of Hormuz that hosts IRGC naval and missile bases, came the same day Qatari mediators reported progress in indirect US–Iran talks, and on the eve of the US midterm elections after which President Donald Trump has been expected to decide on wider strikes.
The details, as reported by CNN, USA Today and the Journal via multiple relays, are still thin on damage. One US official said the strike came in response to Iran firing at a US aircraft; another described it as "a defensive measure for Iranians using surface-to-air missiles against US assets." The Journal reported that the US has carried out other such limited strikes in recent weeks without announcing them, to avoid signalling a return to major combat. Iran's state-affiliated Fars agency reported several explosions heard on Qeshm in the early hours of Tuesday local time, also heard on nearby Hengam Island and in Bandar Abbas. The IRGC claimed it shot down two US reconnaissance drones over Qeshm and destroyed an MQ-9 east of the strait — claims US Central Command has disputed in part and that remain unverified. Neither government has confirmed a strike on the record, and no targets, damage or casualties have been independently established.
Each side's public posture points in a different direction. Washington's line, through unnamed officials, is that this was protective, not escalatory — and one person familiar with the matter told CNN the administration deliberately kept it under wraps "in an effort not to overstate the defensive move." Tehran's deputy foreign minister, Kazem Gharibabadi, downplayed the incident as part of an "ongoing war" while reserving the right to defend itself, and parliamentary speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf warned early Tuesday that any enemy miscalculation would meet an "unpredictable" military and strategic response. At the same time, the diplomacy track moved: Qatar's foreign ministry said its mediation team had returned to Doha after talks in Tehran, that "clear progress is emerging," and that both sides are reviewing the mediators' proposals; CNN cited diplomats saying responses are expected within two days. Vice President JD Vance said Monday the two sides have "made some progress" toward an off-ramp. Trump, for his part, told Fox News the war is "a very soft war," said a deal "could happen," and again raised Pickaxe Mountain, the suspected underground nuclear site, as a target he could hit "in one hour" whenever he wants.
For ordinary people, the stakes run through fuel prices. Oil rose in early Asian trading Tuesday after the strike news broke, after falling Monday on hopes for a deal — and CNN notes gasoline and diesel prices are on track to be the most expensive of any US Election Day in history. The strait, through which about 20 million barrels of oil a day passed before the war, is the reason a limited strike on one island moves pump prices on another continent. The two-day Hormuz reopening offer Tehran has floated — blockade lifted, sanctions waived, frozen assets released, then the strait reopens — remains the shape of any deal, and Washington's answer is still outstanding.
In short: a limited, unannounced US strike on Qeshm that Washington calls defensive and Tehran calls part of an ongoing war, landing hours before Americans vote, while Qatari mediators say the talks are making real progress and expect answers within two days. The strike and the talks are now racing each other.
Sources:
Source: cnn.com.

item.title: Israel's opposition agrees on Eisenkot — but the coalition maths still doesn't work
item.description:
Israel's opposition leaders held their first joint meeting since the October 27 election on Tuesday morning in Herzliya, and came out with a single candidate and a plan: all participating parties will recommend Yashar leader Gadi Eisenkot to President Isaac Herzog for the first mandate to form a government, their negotiating teams will immediately begin drafting guiding principles and coalition agreements, and they will move to replace the Knesset speaker at the first opportunity.
The details, as reported by Israel RealTime and Anadolu via DailyImroz, show agreement on the candidate but not on the coalition. The joint statement, issued under the Change and Reform parties, pledged a "National Emergency Government" and a "Zionist government" built on Eisenkot's four principles, and accused Likud and Netanyahu of a campaign to delegitimise the election results. Former prime minister Naftali Bennett said his Beyachad party "will fully mobilize to help Gadi Eisenkot form a government as soon as possible." But the arithmetic is unchanged: Netanyahu's bloc holds 53 of 120 seats, the Jewish opposition 48, the Arab-led parties 19, and 61 are needed. Yair Golan's position in favour of a government with the Arab parties remained a minority view at the meeting, Avigdor Liberman still refuses a government that includes or depends on Arab parties, and Joint List chairman Yousef Jabareen told CNN he will not join a coalition because he "cannot take responsibility for military actions against our Palestinian people." A separate wrinkle: Liberman said his party will back Yair Lapid for Knesset speaker, a move Channel 12 analyst Amit Segal read as pushing toward another election — while figures in Eisenkot's own party said Lapid will not become speaker, arguing it would kill almost all chances of forming a government.
Each side's argument is about legitimacy versus arithmetic. The opposition says it has a parliamentary majority for change and a decisive public vote, and that replacing the speaker and taking the mandate are the first steps to acting on it. Netanyahu's camp says he must lead any broad government and rejects one dependent on the Arab parties; his bloc, with 53 seats, remains the largest. Herzog begins two days of consultations with factions on Wednesday, starting with the smaller parties, and whoever he taps gets 28 days plus a possible 14-day extension.
For ordinary Israelis, the practical consequence is a caretaker government that stays in place while the deadlock plays out: Netanyahu remains prime minister until a new government is sworn in, and the two routes to 61 — a minority arrangement Liberman has ruled out, or a unity government Eisenkot has ruled out joining under Netanyahu — are both blocked by the people who would have to agree to them. Eisenkot is also due to begin receiving direct Shin Bet protection on Wednesday.
In short: the opposition now speaks with one voice behind Eisenkot and has a plan for the Knesset's first days, but 48 plus Arab recommendations it won't govern on still isn't a coalition — and Wednesday's presidential consultations are where that contradiction gets tested.
Sources:
Source: israelrealtime.com.

item.title: Poland's tribunal assembly convenes today — outcome pending:
item.description:
Judge Anna Korwin-Piotrowska's general assembly of Constitutional Tribunal judges is scheduled for 3:30 PM Warsaw time (8:30 AM CT), with the quorum dispute unresolved — she says 10 of the fixed 15 judges are needed; PiS figures have advised judges not to attend and dispute it is an assembly at all.
New since the night brief: the International Commission of Jurists called on all Polish institutions to resolve the crisis through the rule of law and warned against using police or criminal proceedings to change the court's composition; President Nawrocki convened the National Security Council for Tuesday over the tribunal situation, and the Supreme Court president called an extraordinary general assembly of Supreme Court judges the same day. The Prosecutor General has also filed five motions to lift the immunities of tribunal president Święczkowski and his deputy.
Sources:
Source: pollar.news.

item.title: Binance — second withdrawal phase opens Tuesday:
item.description:
Binance's Recovery Update #6, posted at 02:30 UTC Tuesday, reopened withdrawals from 04:00 UTC across nine networks — BNB Smart Chain, Ethereum, Solana, XRP Ledger, Sui, Arbitrum, Optimism, Tron and Base — rolled out progressively by asset and network after security checks, with lower-liquidity tokens still paused.
The exchange's full zero-knowledge proof for the October 31 reserves snapshot is now complete, letting holders of 10 major tokens (BTC, ETH, XRP, BNB, SOL, USDT, USDC, USD1, RLUSD, ZEC) verify their balances are backed 1:1, and it says about 95% of the $6.3 billion stolen has been replaced from its own balance sheet, with the remaining 5% mostly low-liquidity tokens. Founder statements add that Binance "did not borrow money" to cover the loss.
Another reserves snapshot is due Wednesday. Caveat as before: these are the company's own statements and a self-verifiable proof, not an independent audit.
Sources:
Source: catenaa.com.

item.title: Russian bombs kill at least 26 at a humanitarian aid centre in Zaporizhzhia
item.description:
Russian aerial bombs struck a school being used as a humanitarian aid distribution centre and a nearby shelter in the front-line village of Komyshuvakha, in Ukraine's Zaporizhzhia region, on Monday, killing at least 26 people and injuring five, according to Ukrainian officials. The toll rose through the day — from an initial 18 reported by President Volodymyr Zelensky, to 24 confirmed by Ukraine's State Emergency Service (DSNS), to 26 in Zelensky's Monday evening address — and officials warn it could rise further, with around 20 people still reported missing.
The details, as reported by the DSNS via Political.org, BBC News via EuropeSays, and Deutsche Welle via Augerton, describe a double strike. Russian forces first hit the school building where residents collected humanitarian aid, then dropped nine more bombs — ten in total, several of them reported as 3,000-kilogram weapons — directly on the shelter where people had taken refuge after the first strike. Among the dead are two DSNS rescue workers, Denys Konovalenko and Oleksii Sushchevskyi, both 44, and four police officers, killed after arriving at the scene. Rescue work through the evening was repeatedly interrupted by Russian drone attacks in the area, and responders searched rubble by flashlight as night fell. Komyshuvakha sits about 20 kilometres from the front line. Authorities declared Tuesday, November 3, a day of mourning across the Zaporizhzhia region.
The two sides' positions are, in this case, an accusation met with silence. Zelensky said Russian forces "could not have been unaware" that residents collected aid at the site every week, called the attack "utterly horrific," and framed it as a signal against de-escalation: the strike came the day after the six-day Oleshky humanitarian truce expired, a pause he said had created an opening for further steps toward peace. "With such killings, Russia is sending the exact opposite signal — Russia is counting on further killings," he said. The Russian military had not publicly commented on the attack as of Monday evening. Russia has repeatedly denied deliberately targeting civilians, a standing denial that does not address the specific facts of this strike. The strike itself was in Zaporizhzhia, not Kherson, so it did not technically breach the local Oleshky arrangement — but Ukraine's General Staff said Monday that Russia used that truce to rotate units, fortify positions and move ammunition, and Kyiv's broader argument is that the window the truce opened has now slammed shut.
For ordinary people, the human impact is the point of the target itself: this was not a military depot or a rail yard but the place where residents of a front-line village collected weekly aid — food and essentials for people who have stayed within range of guided bombs. The deaths of the rescue workers and police who came to help, and the drone attacks that kept interrupting the search for survivors, show how the danger compounds after the first explosion. The timing also matters for diplomacy: the strike landed eight days before US-mediated working-level talks between Ukrainian and Russian delegations are due in Abu Dhabi on November 10–11, where, according to US envoy Steve Witkoff, the agenda covers post-war security arrangements, de-escalation and humanitarian initiatives.
In short: at least 26 people are dead after a double bomb strike on an aid centre and shelter in Komyshuvakha, including the rescuers who came to help; Kyiv calls it a deliberate signal against peace, Moscow has said nothing about it, and the toll may still rise as the missing are searched for under drone threat.
Sources:
Source: political.org.

The toll rose through the day — from an initial 18 reported by President Volodymyr Zelensky, to 24 confirmed by Ukraine's State Emergency Service (DSNS), to 26 in Zelensky's Monday evening address — and officials warn it could rise further, with around 20 people still reported missing.

The details, as reported by the DSNS via Political.org, BBC News via EuropeSays, and Deutsche Welle via Augerton, describe a double strike. Russian forces first hit the school building where residents collected humanitarian aid, then dropped nine more bombs — ten in total, several of them reported as 3,000-kilogram weapons — directly on the shelter where people had taken refuge after the first strike. Among the dead are two DSNS rescue workers, Denys Konovalenko and Oleksii Sushchevskyi, both 44, and four police officers, killed after arriving at the scene. Rescue work through the evening was repeatedly interrupted by Russian drone attacks in the area, and responders searched rubble by flashlight as night fell. Komyshuvakha sits about 20 kilometres from the front line. Authorities declared Tuesday, November 3, a day of mourning across the Zaporizhzhia region.

The two sides' positions are, in this case, an accusation met with silence. Zelensky said Russian forces "could not have been unaware" that residents collected aid at the site every week, called the attack "utterly horrific," and framed it as a signal against de-escalation: the strike came the day after the six-day Oleshky humanitarian truce expired, a pause he said had created an opening for further steps toward peace. "With such killings, Russia is sending the exact opposite signal — Russia is counting on further killings," he said. The Russian military had not publicly commented on the attack as of Monday evening. Russia has repeatedly denied deliberately targeting civilians, a standing denial that does not address the specific facts of this strike. The strike itself was in Zaporizhzhia, not Kherson, so it did not technically breach the local Oleshky arrangement — but Ukraine's General Staff said Monday that Russia used that truce to rotate units, fortify positions and move ammunition, and Kyiv's broader argument is that the window the truce opened has now slammed shut.

For ordinary people, the human impact is the point of the target itself: this was not a military depot or a rail yard but the place where residents of a front-line village collected weekly aid — food and essentials for people who have stayed within range of guided bombs. The deaths of the rescue workers and police who came to help, and the drone attacks that kept interrupting the search for survivors, show how the danger compounds after the first explosion. The timing also matters for diplomacy: the strike landed eight days before US-mediated working-level talks between Ukrainian and Russian delegations are due in Abu Dhabi on November 10–11, where, according to US envoy Steve Witkoff, the agenda covers post-war security arrangements, de-escalation and humanitarian initiatives.

In short: at least 26 people are dead after a double bomb strike on an aid centre and shelter in Komyshuvakha, including the rescuers who came to help; Kyiv calls it a deliberate signal against peace, Moscow has said nothing about it, and the toll may still rise as the missing are searched for under drone threat.

item.title: Poland's court crisis deepens: Tusk demands Nawrocki swear in the judges, prosecutors get five complaints, Tuesday's assembly is the test
item.description:
Poland's Constitutional Tribunal standoff moved from street confrontation to legal and political trench warfare on Monday, with both camps now accusing the other of a coup — and Tuesday's general assembly of tribunal judges shaping up as the next flashpoint. Prime Minister Donald Tusk wrote on X on Monday that the conflict "can be resolved simply and without amending the constitution" if President Karol Nawrocki recognises the judges lawfully elected by the Sejm and lets them take up their posts, accusing Nawrocki of choosing "a forced confrontation that could cost Poland dearly" and accusing PiS leader Jarosław Kaczyński of orchestrating a destabilisation campaign with the president's cooperation.
The details, as reported by Reuters, Euronews and Pollar, show how fast the crisis has formalised. On Friday night, the tribunal's longest-serving judge, Anna Korwin-Piotrowska, suspended tribunal president Bogdan Święczkowski and his deputy and declared herself acting president; Nawrocki cut short a trip to Africa, returned to Warsaw, and was filmed pushing past Korwin-Piotrowska at the tribunal doors, calling the events "a forcible takeover of a constitutional body." By Monday afternoon, Warsaw prosecutors had received five formal complaints about the October 30–31 events: the PiS parliamentary club alleges Korwin-Piotrowska and two others attacked a constitutional organ by exceeding their powers, while a regional councillor alleges Nawrocki forcibly entered the tribunal and judges' bodily integrity was violated. A general assembly of tribunal judges chaired by Korwin-Piotrowska is scheduled for Tuesday, but Reuters notes its ability to decide anything depends on securing a quorum of 10 of the court's 15 judges. The European Commission has effectively sided with Tusk, with Justice Commissioner Michael McGrath affirming parliament's right to appoint judges and saying the tribunal must function in line with the constitution and EU case law; the US ambassador in Warsaw, Tom Rose, said it was not his place to interfere but expressed concern for Poland's stability, security and democratic future.
Each side's argument runs in opposite directions from the same facts. Tusk's camp says the Sejm lawfully elected new judges, Nawrocki refused to swear them in, and the tribunal under Święczkowski — appointed during PiS rule — blocked them from hearing cases, so the suspension restores a court that can function; Tusk told the nation Saturday that "a politician cannot enter a court or tribunal and give orders or intimidate judges, even if he is the president." Nawrocki's camp says the suspension itself was unlawful, the takeover was forced, and the president was defending a constitutional organ — a framing echoed by former Russian president Dmitry Medvedev's claim that a coup took place in Poland, which Tusk cited in his Monday post as evidence of who benefits from the chaos. The dispute dates to 2015, when PiS appointed judges to seats already filled, and the court has been effectively paralysed since, with nearly 1,000 pending cases.
For ordinary people, the stakes are less abstract than a judges' roster: Reuters notes the crisis could affect next year's parliamentary election and push Poland closer to the Trump administration and away from the European mainstream, while economists at Polish bank PKO BP warned Monday that a prolonged dispute could raise institutional risks and weigh on assessments of Poland's creditworthiness. The tribunal's own functioning matters too — a court that could not even adopt its 2027 budget this year now faces a Tuesday meeting that may or may not reach quorum.
In short: Tusk gave Nawrocki a simple off-ramp on Monday — swear in the Sejm-elected judges — prosecutors are now holding five competing complaints, Brussels has backed Tusk, and everything hinges on whether Tuesday's judges' assembly can muster 10 of 15 judges.
Sources:
Source: srnnews.com.

item.title: Israel: Liberman backs Eisenkot, Eisenkot rules out any Netanyahu government — but the arithmetic still doesn't add up
item.description:
Israel's opposition hardened into a clearer shape on Monday, even as the numbers showed why forming a government remains difficult. Yisrael Beytenu chairman Avigdor Liberman announced his party will recommend Yashar leader Gadi Eisenkot to form the next government, saying, in remarks reported by i24NEWS and Channel 12 analyst Amit Segal, that "the world will turn upside down before I sit with Netanyahu," even if offered first place in a rotation — and ruling out a minority government dependent on Arab-party support. Separately, public broadcaster KAN reported Eisenkot himself has ruled out serving in any Netanyahu-led government, even if US President Donald Trump asks him, telling a closed-door meeting: "I will not sit in a government led by Netanyahu."
The details, as reported by Clash Report, The Cradle and the Insight International/Anadolu account of the KAN report, leave the opposition one seat short of a governing majority on its own terms. Netanyahu's bloc won 53 of 120 Knesset seats on October 27, the Jewish opposition parties 48, and the Arab-led parties 19; a government needs 61. Liberman's 7 seats bring the Jewish opposition to 48 recommendations for Eisenkot, and the two Arab lists are expected to recommend him too, taking him to a projected 67 recommendations — but recommendations are not coalition seats, and Liberman refuses a government that includes or relies on Arab parties, while the Joint List says it will help replace Netanyahu but will not join a government. Opposition leaders are due to meet Tuesday to coordinate; President Isaac Herzog begins consultations Wednesday, starting with the smaller parties, and whoever he taps gets 28 days, plus a possible 14-day extension, to win a confidence vote. Netanyahu, for his part, said Monday he is open to talks on a broad government but insisted he must lead it, and rejected a coalition dependent on the Arab parties.
For ordinary Israelis, the practical consequence of the deadlock is continuity without resolution: Netanyahu stays on as caretaker prime minister until a new government is sworn in, and the two live alternatives — a minority arrangement Liberman has ruled out, or a unity government Eisenkot has now ruled out joining under Netanyahu — are both blocked by the very people who would have to agree to them. The viral claim circulating Monday that Eisenkot will be sworn in on November 10 is false: that is the new Knesset's opening session, not a swearing-in.
In short: the opposition now has a single candidate in Eisenkot and a firm set of refusals from both Liberman and Eisenkot himself, but 48 Jewish-opposition seats plus Arab recommendations that Liberman won't govern on still leaves no agreed 61 — and Tuesday's opposition meeting is where that contradiction has to be faced.
Sources:
Source: clashreport.com.

item.title: Saudi–Houthi exchange, Monday evening:
item.description:
The Houthis claimed drone strikes on Dammam airport over the past 48 hours — saying air traffic was disrupted — plus a hit on an early-warning radar in Jizan and a military transport aircraft at Jizan airport; Saudi authorities had not confirmed those claims.
Separately, the Saudi-led coalition said it intercepted two drones over the Riyadh region and a ballistic missile toward the south on Monday. Houthi health officials said coalition strikes on Ras Isa port and a Bajil oil facility in Hodeidah wounded seven civilians (four at the port, three at the facility).
The EU's High Representative issued a statement Monday condemning the Houthis' escalation, including the attack on Aden's Al-Maashiq palace and the renewed siege of Taiz, and noting more than 22 million people in Yemen need assistance. Sources:
Source: political.org.

item.title: Ukraine's refinery war is fully back on — Samara oil hub hit for the fourth time in a month
item.description:
Ukraine's campaign against Russian oil infrastructure, paused for about two weeks under pressure from Washington, is now unmistakably resumed — and Monday brought a fresh strike deep in Russia's Volga region. Ukrainian drones hit the Samara Linear Production and Dispatch Station (LPDS) near Prosvet overnight, the fourth attack on the facility since early October, with NASA satellite imagery analysed by Bloomberg showing a relatively fresh fire at the crude pumping and storage site. The station is a major hub for receiving, storing and blending crude from Tatarstan, Western Siberia and other producing regions into export-grade fuel, including for Russia's armed forces, according to Ukraine's General Staff.
The details, as reported by OilPrice/Bloomberg, the Kyiv Independent and Ukrainian monitoring channels, show a campaign that restarted Friday and has not let up since. The Novokuibyshevsk refinery in the Samara region — one of the Volga's leading refineries and part of Rosneft's Samara group — was hit Friday, the first Ukrainian strike on a Russian refinery since October 15, according to the Wall Street Journal. Over the weekend, Ukrainian drones hit a Rosneft refinery in Bashkortostan and Lukoil's Kstovo (NORSI) refinery in Nizhny Novgorod, where the governor reported "significant damage" to an industrial facility and the regional government urged motorists to "buy fuel only as needed." At Samara, residents of Prosvet reported explosions, footage showed smoke rising from the facility, and the regional governor confirmed air defences were responding to a drone attack without confirming the locations hit. Russia's Defence Ministry said it downed 212 Ukrainian drones overnight across 16 regions, Crimea and the Black and Azov seas — a figure that, like all ministry claims, is not independently verified. The extent of damage at Samara itself is also unconfirmed; the satellite fire is an anomaly, not a damage assessment.
The political argument around the strikes sharpened Monday too. Senior Ukrainian officials confirmed to the Kyiv Independent that Kyiv never agreed to pause strikes on Russian oil sites on October 31 — undercutting the framing of President Donald Trump's "energy ceasefire," which he claimed to have brokered in mid-October. Trump has pressed Kyiv to halt the refinery strikes ahead of Tuesday's US midterm elections, blaming them for record diesel prices; his administration accuses Ukraine of contributing to a diesel crisis that sent US retail prices to record highs in September. Moscow's line, via Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak, is that the strikes are adding to global fuel-market imbalances. Kyiv's position, stated repeatedly, is that it supports a full ceasefire on energy targets — including its own battered power grid — but that Moscow is unwilling to agree to one.
For ordinary people, the most direct measure is at the pump: OilPrice reports the US national average retail diesel price at $6.29 per gallon as of November 2, up from $3.68 a gallon at this time last year — a year ago there was no Middle East war restricting crude and fuel flows from the Gulf. In Ukraine, the other side of the same exchange continues: Russian strikes on energy infrastructure left hundreds of thousands of households without power over the weekend, and Monday's strikes in Kherson (see below) show the front-line war did not pause either.
In short: Ukraine has now hit at least three refineries plus the Samara oil hub since Friday, Kyiv says it never agreed to the pause Trump claimed, and with US diesel at $6.29 a gallon the strikes are now a domestic American political issue as much as a Ukrainian military one — one day before the midterms Trump cited when demanding they stop.
Sources:
Source: oilprice.com.

Russia's Defence Ministry said it downed 212 Ukrainian drones overnight across 16 regions, Crimea and the Black and Azov seas — a figure that, like all ministry claims, is not independently verified. The extent of damage at Samara itself is also unconfirmed; the satellite fire is an anomaly, not a damage assessment.

The political argument around the strikes sharpened Monday too. Senior Ukrainian officials confirmed to the Kyiv Independent that Kyiv never agreed to pause strikes on Russian oil sites on October 31 — undercutting the framing of President Donald Trump's "energy ceasefire," which he claimed to have brokered in mid-October. Trump has pressed Kyiv to halt the refinery strikes ahead of Tuesday's US midterm elections, blaming them for record diesel prices; his administration accuses Ukraine of contributing to a diesel crisis that sent US retail prices to record highs in September. Moscow's line, via Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak, is that the strikes are adding to global fuel-market imbalances. Kyiv's position, stated repeatedly, is that it supports a full ceasefire on energy targets — including its own battered power grid — but that Moscow is unwilling to agree to one.

For ordinary people, the most direct measure is at the pump: OilPrice reports the US national average retail diesel price at $6.29 per gallon as of November 2, up from $3.68 a gallon at this time last year — a year ago there was no Middle East war restricting crude and fuel flows from the Gulf. In Ukraine, the other side of the same exchange continues: Russian strikes on energy infrastructure left hundreds of thousands of households without power over the weekend, and Monday's strikes in Kherson (see below) show the front-line war did not pause either.

In short: Ukraine has now hit at least three refineries plus the Samara oil hub since Friday, Kyiv says it never agreed to the pause Trump claimed, and with US diesel at $6.29 a gallon the strikes are now a domestic American political issue as much as a Ukrainian military one — one day before the midterms Trump cited when demanding they stop.

item.title: Doha has a draft, oil plunges more than 7% — but Washington still hasn't answered, and the clock runs out Tuesday
item.description:
The diplomacy track produced its most concrete movement yet on Monday — and the oil market moved first, hardest, and furthest. Iranian negotiators left Doha on Sunday, but not in a walkout: an official briefed on the talks told Reuters a draft proposal for a deal with the United States is now being circulated, with a follow-up meeting possible. Hours later, crude collapsed: Brent settled near $104.77 a barrel, down 7.6%, and US West Texas Intermediate fell 7.4% to $96.46, back below $100, on the eve of the US midterm elections.
The details, as reported by Reuters, the Associated Press and Iranian officials, show a negotiation that has narrowed to a specific, still-unaccepted offer. Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei said Monday the basis of the talks remains Iran's seven-step plan drawn up in September — the US ends its naval blockade of Iranian ports, Iran reopens the Strait of Hormuz, Washington grants oil-sale waivers and cancels new sanctions, and the sides then move to the nuclear file and other issues — but now condensed so it could be implemented in two days rather than the original seven. The AP adds two conditions not in the morning's coverage: ships would use a route agreed by Iran and Oman and travel under Iranian supervision, and Tehran wants a ceasefire that includes Lebanon. Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi stayed in Doha to exchange messages with Washington via Qatari mediators. On the Iranian side, President Masoud Pezeshkian said Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei has granted the government additional authority to pursue the talks, and Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said a deal is possible if Washington "demonstrates goodwill." Trump, for his part, told reporters Monday that Iran wants to "make a deal and that could happen," while repeating that the US would not strike before Tuesday's vote.
The case for scepticism is not hard to find, and it comes from Tehran itself. Reports Monday note Khamenei has ordered the armed forces to update their target lists and be ready for a geographically unrestricted response to threats — the posture of a leadership preparing for talks to fail, not just succeed. Baghaei himself said Tehran does not expect the US elections to "give birth to a new US," and stressed no final agreement can begin, nor the strait be reopened, unless the blockade ends and Iran's demands are met. The American side has given no public answer to the draft, and the previously reported fallback — a 72-hour post-moratorium strike blueprint drawn up by US and Israeli officials, reported by the New York Times and Axios on October 22 — remains live once Trump's self-imposed no-strike pledge expires with Tuesday's vote.
For ordinary people, the day's oil move is the most tangible link between Doha and daily life: a 7%+ drop unwound a large part of October's war premium, which had pushed Brent to a six-month high — but nothing physical has changed yet. No tanker has moved through a reopened strait, the weekend's mine and projectile incidents in Hormuz remain unattributed, and Goldman Sachs still raised its December Brent forecast to $105 (from $90) on supply risk, warning of $140 in 2027 if Gulf output stays depressed. If the draft becomes a deal, fuel and heating costs could ease; if it collapses after Tuesday, the same prices could run the other way just as fast.
In short: Doha produced a circulating draft and a two-day reopening offer with Iranian supervision of an Oman-agreed route, oil plunged more than 7% on the hope, and Trump says a deal "could happen" — but Washington has not accepted anything, Tehran is simultaneously updating its target lists, and the strike moratorium expires Tuesday, so the whole thing now hinges on an answer that has not come.
Sources:
Source: tbsnews.net.

item.title: Kherson, after the truce:
item.description:
Monday's return to fighting in Kherson got sharper detail than the morning's first reports — a Russian drone hit a medical facility in central Kherson at about 7:40 a.m., damaging rooms and shattering windows with no casualties reported at the clinic, and minutes later a second drone struck a car in the Korabelny district, wounding a 62-year-old woman and a 73-year-old man.
Moscow's response to Kyiv's charge that Russia used the Oleshky pause to fortify: Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said he had no specific information on Russian operations but assumed Ukrainian forces had also used the ceasefire to regroup. Sources:

item.title: Israel — the numbers behind the Eisenkot lead:
item.description:
Joint List leader Yousef Jabareen told The Guardian on Monday his party is ready to help replace Netanyahu but will not join a government, though it would consider supporting one from outside — which matters because Liberman has ruled out a government dependent on Arab-party support.
Ynet projects 60 recommendations for Eisenkot against 46 for Netanyahu when Herzog consults from Wednesday, and reports the ultra-Orthodox United Torah Judaism party is weighing ending its alliance with Netanyahu. Election and security officials rejected Likud's fraud claims, saying the result stands.
None of this is a coalition deal — recommending a candidate is not joining his government, and a viral post claiming Eisenkot will be sworn in November 10 is false: that is the Knesset's opening session, not a swearing-in. Sources:
Source: auraxnews.com.

item.title: Poland — a constitutional crisis, not just the plot case:
item.description:
Friday night's standoff at the Constitutional Tribunal escalated into a full-blown institutional fight Monday.
A judge, Anna Korwin-Piotrowska, suspended the tribunal's president Bogdan Święczkowski and his deputy; President Karol Nawrocki turned his plane around mid-flight over Spain and returned to Warsaw as riot police and protesters gathered; three people were detained. At least three ambassadors have resigned in protest — including Poland's permanent representative to the UN, Krzysztof Szczerski, on Monday, after the ambassadors to China and Romania over the weekend.
A police trade union has demanded answers about the operation's legality, and Rzeczpospolita reports it was planned by senior police leadership, timed for the All Saints' Day weekend while Nawrocki was due abroad. Tusk defended the move Saturday; coalition partners PSL and Poland 2050 are in emergency talks with Nawrocki.
Treat the framing with care: the two English-language outlets carrying this are partisan-leaning, though both cite Rzeczpospolita, a mainstream Polish paper. Sources:
Source: axynewsglobal.com.

item.title: Apple beats in Ternus's first earnings — a record $114.5 billion quarter, with a margin caveat underneath
item.description:
Apple reported fiscal Q4 2026 after the close Monday — the first earnings under new CEO John Ternus — and beat Wall Street on both lines: revenue of $114.5 billion, up 12% year on year, against a consensus of about $113.4 billion, and diluted EPS of $2.10, up 14%, against about $1.99 expected. iPhone revenue hit a September-quarter record of $57.58 billion, up about 17%, Services reached an all-time high of $31.57 billion, up about 10%, and Mac rose to $10.79 billion. For the full fiscal year, revenue reached $479 billion, which Apple called its best fiscal year ever, with $28 billion in operating cash flow and $28 billion returned to shareholders; the board declared a $0.27 dividend payable November 16.
The details, as reported by Apple itself, AppleInsider, the Motley Fool and Zacks, give the beat two complications worth knowing. First, the stock fell 1.83% to $338.32 into the results amid a broader tech sell-off, so the beat landed after a bad session, not a celebratory one. Second, gross margin of 47.9% was down from 50.1% the prior quarter, reflecting rising component costs — and it included a favourable impact of about one percentage point from tariff refunds, worth about $0.05 of the $2.10 EPS. That refund benefit is real money, but it is not obviously recurring, so the underlying margin trend is softer than the headline suggests. Third, the quarter ended September 26, so it captures only the opening weeks of the iPhone 18 cycle — and none of the iPhone Duo, which went on sale in October. Ternus called the Duo "the most transformational iPhone since the original" and pointed to the home lineup and "all-new Siri AI" as the holiday-season story; the real demand test for all of that lands in next quarter's report.
For ordinary people, the practical read is simpler than the market reaction: Apple just posted its biggest September quarter ever on the strength of iPhones and services, its installed base hit a new all-time high, and nothing in this report changes prices or products you can buy — but if you are watching whether the iPhone Duo is a genuine hit or a niche experiment, this report does not answer that yet. Next quarter does.
In short: a record quarter and a clean beat in Ternus's debut, with margin pressure and tariff refunds muddying the quality of the beat — and the iPhone Duo verdict still to come.
Sources:
Source: apple.com.

item.title: Binance — reserve proof now verifiable, next phase Tuesday:
item.description:
Binance completed its zero-knowledge proof-of-reserves verification Monday morning, so holders of the ten fully backed tokens (BTC, ETH, USDT, BNB, SOL, USDC, XRP, USD1, RLUSD, ZEC) can now verify balances 1:1 against the October 31 snapshot; about 95% of the $6.3 billion stolen is covered, the rest in less-liquid tokens still being sourced.
The exchange says it will begin progressively restoring withdrawals for additional networks and assets on Tuesday, with another reserves snapshot Wednesday. Outflows are easing: DeFiLlama put 24-hour net outflows at about $3.29 billion, down from an earlier ~$7 billion peak.
Co-CEO Richard Teng warned Monday about impersonation scams offering "priority processing" of withdrawals — Binance says it never charges to speed one up or contacts users first. Sources:
Source: theblock.co.

item.title: Russell Brand — defence closing concluded Monday, jury goes out Tuesday:
item.description:
Defence barrister Ian Winter KC finished his closing speech at Southwark Crown Court on Monday, urging jurors to separate Brand's sexual behaviour from the question of crime: "It is not criminal to treat women unkindly before, during or after sex.
It is not, I am afraid, criminal to be disrespectful or rude or acting like a crazy idiot. If there is consent it is lawful."
He argued Brand "genuinely believed" the women were consenting, that there is "no evidence" he is "some kind of psychopath who rapes people and thinks it's normal," and that the complainants were "thoroughly contaminated" by the 2023 Channel 4 Dispatches documentary and Times/Sunday Times reporting that prompted them to come forward — leaving a "quagmire of doubt and inaccurate recollection." Brand, 51, denies three counts of rape, three counts of sexual assault and one count of attempted indecent assault against six women, spanning 1999–2009.
The judge's legal directions come next, with the jury expected to begin deliberating Tuesday, November 3; unanimous verdicts are required at this stage. Nothing here is a finding of guilt.
Sources:
Source: aapnews.aap.com.au.

item.title: After the Oleshky truce: Kyiv says Russia used the pause to dig in, and the drone war is back at full volume
item.description:
The six-day humanitarian truce around Oleshky ended Sunday night without a successor arrangement, and Monday morning brought Kyiv's sharpest charge yet about how it was used: Ukraine's General Staff said Russian forces spent the pause strengthening their positions rather than just holding fire. The claim, carried by Reuters, is the first official Ukrainian assessment of the ceasefire's military side — and it arrived on a morning when the wider war showed no sign of pausing at all.
The details, as reported by Reuters and Ukraine's air force, show both halves of that story. The General Staff said it had recorded rotations of Russian units, fortification of positions, expanded anti-drone measures along roads, and increased logistics activity, including ammunition deliveries, during the October 27–November 1 pause. Ukraine's 34th Separate Marine Brigade "Borysfen" echoed the warning in a video address, telling Kherson residents not to ignore air-raid sirens and saying there were reasons to expect an intensification of hostilities. Kherson governor Oleksandr Prokudin said Russian forces had shelled and attacked with drones and aircraft 16 settlements in Ukrainian-controlled parts of the region, including the city of Kherson itself, in the 24 hours to 0400 GMT Monday — and the city's military administration reported a drone strike in central Kherson on Monday, with no casualties reported. Russia has not publicly responded to the reinforcement charge; its only praise so far has been for how the humanitarian operation itself was conducted.
Overnight, the air war resumed at scale. Ukraine's air force said Russia launched 193 drones during the night of November 1–2, including 75 jet-powered Shahed-type drones, and that air defences shot down or suppressed 154 of them by 08:00, with hits recorded at 26 locations and debris falling at nine more. Local reports tallied the human cost: in the Vinnytsia region, a drone hit a dormitory housing internally displaced people from Donetsk, killing a 13-year-old girl and a woman and injuring six more, including four children; in Sumy region, a 70-year-old woman was killed when a drone hit a car; in Kharkiv region, 11 people were injured, including a 3-year-old girl; and in Odesa and Zaporizhzhia, further injuries and damaged homes were reported. The previous night had been heavier still — Reuters reported Sunday strikes on energy facilities in four regions that left hundreds of thousands of households without power, with Ukraine's air force saying it downed 371 of 433 Russian long-range drones, while Kyiv said it hit the Kamensky plant in Russia's Rostov region and the governor of Nizhny Novgorod reported "significant damage" to an industrial facility there. Russia's Defence Ministry, for its part, said it downed 235 Ukrainian drones overnight.
There is also a stranger front opening: the alert systems themselves. Ukraine's air force confirmed Sunday that its Air Alarm app was hacked with false radiation-threat alerts minutes after the truce expired, with Kyiv's strategic-communications centre blaming Russia — an attribution that is Kyiv's claim, not independently verified. A roundup of the weekend's incidents reports that public alert systems in Russia also sent false chemical and nuclear warnings after what both sides described as cyberattacks on their mobile alert apps. Neither side's claim about the other's hack has been independently confirmed, and both are worth treating as wartime claims rather than established fact.
For ordinary people, the picture is bleakly familiar: a humanitarian experiment that evacuated nearly 800 people and held without violations, according to both sides' own human-rights officials, is now being argued over as a military episode — while the energy strikes, the drone alerts and the hacked warning apps all point the same way, toward another winter in which power, heat and trustworthy warnings are all under pressure.
In short: Kyiv says Russia used the Oleshky pause to rotate troops, fortify positions and move ammunition, and is warning Kherson residents to expect heavier fighting — as overnight drone exchanges, civilian casualties in several regions, and duelling claims of hacked alert apps show the wider war never actually stopped.
Sources:
Source: kwsn.com.
