item.title: Doha talks produce a draft — and oil traders bet on it before any tanker moves safely
item.description:
Indirect talks in Doha between Iranian negotiators and Qatari mediators produced something new on Monday: a draft proposal now being circulated, with a follow-up meeting possible, according to an official briefed on the talks who spoke to Reuters. Iranian negotiators have left Doha for now, but the talks are not declared dead — and oil markets moved first, falling more than 4% on Monday on hopes that the Strait of Hormuz, the waterway at the centre of the whole standoff, might actually reopen.
The details, as reported by Reuters and the maritime press, show a negotiation that has narrowed to a concrete, if still unaccepted, offer. Iran has proposed reopening the strait within two days of Washington meeting its conditions — shortened from an earlier seven-day timeline during the Doha sessions, according to reports of the talks. Tehran's conditions, as stated by Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi and security chief Mohsen Rezaei, include sanctions relief, the release of more than $6 billion in frozen Iranian assets, restored oil waivers, an end to the US naval blockade and maritime interdictions, and fewer US forces in the region. Araghchi said Sunday the talks were "ongoing and progressing" but had reached no final conclusion, and stressed there are no direct US–Iran talks at this stage. On the American side, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Saturday that President Donald Trump had made no final decision on further strikes but preferred a diplomatic solution, and Axios reported Trump told Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Saturday he preferred to give diplomacy more time. The Guardian's framing, carried in earlier coverage, still holds: Gulf officials are braced for the worst after Tuesday's US midterm elections, when the US moratorium on strikes against Iran is set to expire.
The market reaction was swift — and, by the analysts' own admission, ahead of the facts on the water. Reuters reports Brent crude fell $4.79, or 4.2%, to $108.64 a barrel by 1020 GMT Monday, with US West Texas Intermediate down 4.2% to $99.71, after Brent ended October at its highest level in six months. "The new month brought with it renewed hopes of a breakthrough in the Iranian stalemate," said PVM's Tamas Varga, while KCM Trade's Tim Waterer cautioned that "lingering hopes of some form of diplomatic progress, combined with the absence of any meaningful military escalation over the weekend, have taken some of the immediate heat out of prices for now." The sceptical case got its own numbers Monday: Goldman Sachs raised its December Brent forecast to $105 from $90 on supply risks, and warned Brent could jump to $140 in 2027 if Gulf output stays 3.5 million barrels per day below its 2025 average; ADNOC's chief executive said the world has drained nearly 1 billion barrels from inventories since the war disrupted Hormuz shipping. Seven OPEC+ producers, including Saudi Arabia, Russia and Iraq, agreed Sunday to keep December output targets unchanged, with another meeting set for November 29.
Meanwhile the waterway itself has not gone quiet. The weekend's incidents — a UAE-owned tug reported partially sinking after a projectile strike, a tanker hit by two projectiles near Ras Al Khafji, and Iran's Revolutionary Guard claiming two tankers exploded after hitting mines on an unauthorised route — remain unverified in their attribution, and the Institute for the Study of War assesses Iran likely struck a vessel in the strait on November 1 as part of its effort to disrupt civilian shipping and pressure Washington. No new vessel strike was confirmed early Monday.
For ordinary people, the oil move is the most direct link between Doha and daily life: if the draft becomes a real reopening, fuel and heating costs could ease from levels driven by months of war-risk premiums; if it collapses after Tuesday's midterms, Goldman’s $140 scenario is a reminder of how fast the same prices could run the other way. For now, traders are pricing hope, not passage — no tanker has yet moved through a reopened strait.
In short: Doha produced a circulating draft and a two-day reopening offer that Washington has not accepted, oil fell more than 4% on the hope, but the strait is still effectively closed, the tanker attacks of the weekend are still unattributed, and everything now hinges on Washington's answer and what happens after Tuesday's midterms.
Sources:
Source: kitco.com.

item.title: Saudi–Houthi exchange: missile intercepted, southern cities alerted, and a port strike's civilian toll
item.description:
The Saudi–Houthi exchange continued into Monday morning on both sides of the border: the Saudi-led coalition said it intercepted a Houthi ballistic missile aimed at the kingdom's southern region, Saudi civil defence issued and then lifted alerts for four southern and western cities, and the Houthis reported seven civilians injured in coalition strikes on a Red Sea port and an oil facility in Yemen.
The details, as reported by Reuters, Xinhua and Houthi-run media, show a familiar pattern with a newly documented civilian cost. Reuters reports Saudi civil defence said on Monday that the threat had passed shortly after issuing alerts for Khamis Mushait, Abha, Taif and Najran, amid weeks of escalating hostilities; the coalition later said it had intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile launched by the Iran-aligned Houthis toward the southern region. The coalition had already said Sunday it intercepted a drone and a ballistic missile toward the same region. On the Yemeni side, Houthi health ministry spokesperson Anees al-Asbahi said coalition strikes on Sunday hit Ras Isa port in Hodeidah province, injuring four civilians, and an oil company station in the Bajil district, injuring three more — figures that come from Houthi officials and have not been independently verified, and which the coalition has not commented on specifically. Houthi-run al-Masirah TV had earlier reported the Ras Isa strikes hit a pier and a moored commercial vessel, plus a telecommunications facility southeast of Saada. Houthi military spokesman Yahya Sarea claimed 75 air and missile strikes hit eight provinces over 24 hours and put the total since the latest escalation began at 3,830 — again, Houthi figures, not independently verified.
The two sides' stated targets tell the story of the escalation's logic. The Houthis have repeatedly targeted Saudi airports, air defence facilities and energy infrastructure, including the Shaybah oilfield and the East-West pipeline and Yanbu export facilities, according to Reuters; Saudi strikes have concentrated on Houthi-held ports, fuel infrastructure and command sites in Hodeidah and elsewhere. The human impact beyond the battlefield is now measurable in a different register: the Philippines' Department of Migrant Workers said Monday it has extended 6,873 services to 5,257 overseas Filipino workers across Saudi Arabia as strikes intensified, after an OFW was killed by missile fragments when Saudi defences intercepted a Houthi drone targeting the Shaybah oilfield. The UN figures cited in Houthi coverage put more than 300,000 people displaced within Yemen by the renewed fighting.
For ordinary people in southern Saudi Arabia, the alerts-then-all-clear rhythm is itself the disruption — warnings for cities like Abha and Taif, followed by interceptions, followed by silence — while in Yemen's Hodeidah province, a working port and an oil station are the places where the war lands on civilian livelihoods.
In short: Monday brought another intercepted Houthi missile and alerts across four Saudi cities, matched by Houthi claims of seven civilians injured at Ras Isa port and a Bajil oil facility — the same tit-for-tat exchange, with the civilian and migrant-worker toll now more clearly documented than the military claims on either side.
Sources:
Source: duke.fm.

item.title: Israel's coalition race sharpens: Liberman backs Eisenkot, Netanyahu keeps unity door ajar
item.description:
Israel's post-election deadlock moved decisively on Monday — toward Gadi Eisenkot, not toward a Netanyahu-led government — while Netanyahu himself kept a second, contradictory track open: reported interest in a unity government with Eisenkot, guaranteed by Trump and Herzog, even as he publicly denies planning one.
The details, as reported by Kan, Channel 12, i24NEWS and the Jerusalem Post via several outlets, show the arithmetic shifting. Yisrael Beytenu chairman Avigdor Liberman confirmed Monday he will recommend Eisenkot to form the next government, saying, "The world will turn upside down before I sit with Netanyahu," even if offered first place in a rotation, and ruling out a minority government as well. Liberman's seven seats matter because the final results give Netanyahu's bloc 53 seats, the Jewish opposition parties 48 and the Arab-led parties 19, with 61 of 120 needed to govern; N12 counts 33 recommendations for Eisenkot from Yashar and B'Yachad, rising to 48 with the Democrats and Yisrael Beytenu, and potentially 67 if the Arab-led parties recommend him as expected. Liberman also proposed former prime minister Yair Lapid as Knesset Speaker, a post the opposition bloc plans to take from Likud's Amir Ohana at the November 10 swearing-in. Meanwhile, Kan reported via a Netanyahu confidant, Dimona mayor Benny Biton, that "Benjamin Netanyahu wants unity… this is neither deception nor an election manoeuvre," with a Likud official saying Trump and Herzog would act as guarantors of an agreement with Eisenkot — a claim that sits uneasily beside Netanyahu's public denials and Likud whip Ofir Katz's November 1 ruling-out of a rotation deal. Eisenkot, for his part, has set conditions for coalition partners and vowed to use his Knesset majority to reverse Netanyahu-era policies, though reports do not specify the four principles he is said to require or the exact policies targeted.
The two sides are therefore arguing about different things: Eisenkot's camp is counting recommendations and planning a legislative programme, while Netanyahu's camp is floating a unity arrangement whose guarantors, terms and very existence are all reported rather than confirmed. President Isaac Herzog receives the final results on Wednesday, November 4, begins consultations that day with smaller parties, meets Yashar and Likud on November 5, and must tap a candidate by November 11, who then gets 28 days, plus a possible 14-day extension, to form a government.
For ordinary Israelis, the stakes are practical: another round of elections if no one reaches 61, versus a government — of whichever shape — that can pass a budget and make decisions on the war, the economy and the host of domestic issues frozen since the election. Liberman's move makes the Eisenkot-first path the most likely one to be tried first; it does not make it a done deal, given his own long refusal to sit with Arab-led parties, whose recommendations Eisenkot may still need.
In short: Liberman's backing puts Eisenkot on course to get the first mandate from Herzog, with consultations starting Wednesday — while Netanyahu's reported unity feeler, with Trump and Herzog as guarantors, remains unconfirmed and publicly denied, leaving the minority-government-versus-unity-government choice exactly where it was, only with the numbers now leaning Eisenkot's way.
Sources:
Source: clashreport.com.

item.title: Apple — Q4 earnings after the close today:
item.description:
Apple reports fiscal Q4 earnings after the market closes Monday, November 2 — the first major earnings test for new CEO John Ternus, who took over from Tim Cook in September.
Analysts expect roughly $113.4 billion in revenue (up ~11% year on year) and EPS of $1.99. No new product launch is attached to the report; the September quarter captures only a limited period of iPhone 18 Pro sales.
Sources:
Source: tipranks.com.

item.title: Nvidia — AI Day Seoul announced for November 9–10:
item.description:
Nvidia announced November 2 it will hold Nvidia AI Day Seoul 2026 at COEX in Seoul, November 9–10, showcasing agentic AI, physical AI and AI infrastructure, with a keynote plenary on November 9 featuring robotics VP Deepu Talla on Isaac, Cosmos and AI factories, and 20 partner companies presenting.

item.title: Ivanti deadline is TODAY — patch and rebuild, don't just patch:
item.description:
The federal deadline for Ivanti Connect Secure CVE-2026-111357 (CVSS 8.8, missing authentication for a critical function) falls Monday, November 2.
It is one of three flaws chained by the previously unknown actor UTA0576, tracked by Volexity, to reach root on VPN appliances without logging in — the chain ran from October 3 against even a fully patched appliance. Fixes are 25.1.1.3 and 22.8R2.6 (shipped October 29); CISA requires forensic triage for this one, not only a patch, and warns its Integrity Checker Tool may miss this activity — so affected organisations face rebuilds, not just upgrades.
The second flaw in the chain, CVE-2026-118527 (4.3), is due November 13. Sources:
Source: securityweek.com.

item.title: Binance — reserve proof now verifiable, SAFU Bitcoin halved, next withdrawal phase Tuesday:
item.description:
Binance's Recovery Update #5 says the full zero-knowledge proof for its October 31 proof-of-reserves snapshot is complete, so holders of the ten fully backed tokens (BTC, ETH, USDT, BNB, SOL, USDC, XRP, USD1, RLUSD, ZEC) can now verify their own balances; the exchange says about 95% of the stolen assets are covered.
CoinTelegraph reports Binance's disclosed SAFU Bitcoin wallet held about 7,500 BTC (~$583 million) on Monday, down from about 15,000 BTC before a 7,499 BTC transfer Saturday linked to the partial deployment of its user-protection fund — with no stated timeline for replenishing it. The next withdrawal phase is planned for November 3, with another snapshot covering more tokens planned for Wednesday.
Separately, DeFiLlama data cited by Bitcoin.com shows Binance's tracked assets down about $16.6 billion since the October 29 hack ($144.9B to ~$128.3B), while Binance's own count put Sunday's net outflow at $3.64 billion ($4.65B withdrawn, $1.01B deposited in the first 9.5 hours) — the two counts measure different things, so don't read them as contradicting each other. Sources:
Source: cointelegraph.com.

item.title: Russell Brand — defence closing underway Monday, jury retires Tuesday:
item.description:
Defence barrister Ian Winter KC began his closing speech at Southwark Crown Court on Monday, arguing that 2023 reporting of sexual-misconduct allegations in a Channel 4 Dispatches documentary and Times/Sunday Times stories had "poisoned the well of justice" by prompting the women to come forward, and that the complainants were "not random, not independent" but "thoroughly contaminated" by the programme.
He told jurors: "Living a highly promiscuous life is entirely lawful however morally distasteful you may find it," and asked why only three rapes were alleged in ten years. Brand, 51, denies three charges of rape, three counts of sexual assault and one count of attempted indecent assault against six women, spanning 1999–2009.
The prosecution closed Friday, arguing Brand treated consent as an "obstacle to remove or ignore"; the jury is expected to begin deliberating Tuesday, November 3, with unanimous verdicts required at this stage. Brand denies all charges; nothing here is a finding of guilt.
Sources:
Source: theoldhamtimes.co.uk.

item.title: The truce that held — and the refusal that ended it
item.description:
The war's longest local ceasefire expired Sunday night, and the reason it will not continue is now on the record: a senior Ukrainian official told AFP that Kyiv's Foreign Ministry offered to extend the six-day Oleshky truce and Russia refused. The pause around the Russian-occupied town of Oleshky, in effect from October 27 to November 1, ended with no reported violations — but with no successor arrangement, and with Kherson residents bracing for fighting to resume.
The details, as reported by AFP and carried by The Leaders Online and France 24, show a final day that mixed relief with dread. Ukraine's military evacuated 167 more people Sunday from threatened areas of southern Kherson region before the deadline, and human rights commissioner Dmytro Lubinets confirmed afterward that "the ceasefire, which was in effect from October 27 to November 1, has ended," calling it "an important step in our joint humanitarian efforts." Kherson governor Oleksandr Prokudin urged residents to stay out of the Dnipro "red zones" and to respond immediately to attack warnings. One Kherson resident told AFP the truce had been a "breath of fresh air"; a Ukrainian officer, speaking anonymously, warned the fighting could be "worse than before," saying Russian forces had used the calm to amass troops, move ammunition and reconnoitre Ukrainian positions with surveillance drones. Minutes after the truce ended, Ukraine's air force said its Air Alarm app had probably been subjected to hostile interference after false radiation-threat alerts appeared — spokesman Yuriy Ignat confirmed to AFP that the app had been hacked, and Ukraine's strategic-communications centre blamed Russia, though that attribution is Kyiv's claim, not independently verified.
The two sides are now talking past each other about what comes next. Kyiv's position, as Zelenskyy put it in a Fox News interview Sunday, is transactional: Ukraine would stop hitting Russian oil refineries — as President Donald Trump has demanded — if Washington supplied powerful Patriot interceptor missiles, or if Russia stopped hitting Ukraine's energy system. Moscow, for its part, has praised only the Oleshky operation itself — Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Russia had a positive view of how it was conducted — while Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov insisted initial peace talks should be trilateral, involving only Moscow, Kyiv and Washington, excluding European nations. AFP reports US-mediated talks between Russia and Ukraine are set to resume this month, having been effectively frozen since the United States and Israel launched joint strikes on Iran in February. Pope Leo, who had pressed for the Oleshky truce, said he hoped the cooperation would "strengthen the desire for dialogue and lead to new concrete peace initiatives."
For ordinary people, the end of the truce is the return of danger to a place that had six quiet days — and, beyond Kherson, the continuation of the energy war that left hundreds of thousands of Ukrainian homes without power Sunday after Russian strikes on infrastructure in four regions, with Kyiv under emergency outages for much of the day. Zelenskyy has said Russia is trying to take maximum advantage of Ukraine's shortage of ballistic-missile interceptors, which is why the Patriot offer matters: it ties the refinery-strike question directly to the air-defence gap ordinary Ukrainians feel every night.
In short: the Oleshky truce ended Sunday having held without violations, but Russia refused Kyiv's offer to extend it, leaving the mechanism Kyiv wants to keep alive with no second use agreed — while Zelenskyy offered a refinery-strike halt in exchange for Patriot missiles, trilateral talks are due to resume this month, and Kherson residents are back under attack warnings.
Sources:
Source: theleaders-online.com.

item.title: Doha talks grind on — while the waterway they are about keeps getting hit
item.description:
Indirect talks in Doha between Iranian negotiators and Qatari mediators ran through a third day Sunday with still no agreement on reopening the Strait of Hormuz — and the gap between diplomacy and events on the water widened again, with a UAE-owned tug reported partially sinking after a projectile strike and another tanker hit overnight in the northern Gulf.
The details, as reported by Reuters, AP and the maritime press, show a negotiation that has narrowed to one question: what Washington does next. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Sunday that Tehran was prepared for both defence and diplomacy, that consultations with mediators were continuing, and that the outcome depended on Washington's responses to Iran's questions — including the release of more than $6 billion in frozen Iranian assets and the lifting of sanctions on Iranian oil exports. Araghchi reiterated that there are no direct US–Iran talks at this stage and no final outcome has been reached, while calling a letter from US Vice President JD Vance a "positive step." US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Saturday that President Donald Trump had not made a final decision on further strikes but preferred a diplomatic solution, and that talks with Tehran had "actually never stopped." The Guardian reports Gulf officials are "braced for the worst" ahead of Tuesday's US midterm elections, after which the US moratorium on strikes against Iran is set to expire.
Meanwhile, the strikes did not pause for the talks. UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) reported that an Emirati-owned offshore tug, identified by security consultancy Vanguard Tech as the Selat Storm, was hit by a projectile just after 1500 UTC Sunday northwest of the Musandam Peninsula, with a passing vessel relaying its mayday call and the tug reported "partially sinking"; the crew's status was not reported. Overnight Sunday, UKMTO reported a tanker hit by two projectiles about 70 nautical miles east of Ras Al Khafji, Saudi Arabia, with all crew accounted for — at least the fifth energy vessel hit by suspected Iranian strikes since Thursday, according to the Maritime Executive. Separately, Iran's Revolutionary Guard Navy claimed two oil tankers, including a supertanker, exploded after hitting mines on an unauthorised route — a claim carried by Iranian state media and several outlets but not independently verified, and it is unclear whether it describes the same incidents UKMTO reported. The Institute for the Study of War assesses that Iran likely struck a vessel in the strait on November 1 as part of its effort to disrupt civilian shipping and pressure Washington, and notes Iran remains the only threat to civilian shipping there.
For ordinary people, the stakes are the same ones that have driven this whole standoff: energy prices and winter supply. The Straits daily brief put Brent at $113.43 on Sunday, with shipping through the strait running far below pre-war levels, and every new strike — even one on a small tug, even one with no confirmed casualties — feeds the war-risk premiums and freight costs that eventually reach fuel pumps and heating bills. The Al Mayeda case, confirmed by owner Nakilat on Sunday and covered in the evening brief, is the sharpest version of that worry: a Qatari gas carrier hit reportedly hours after Tehran had cleared its passage, which is why shippers now doubt whether any clearance, or any deal, actually makes the waterway safe.
In short: Doha's third day ended with Araghchi saying Iran is ready for diplomacy or defence and Rubio saying Trump has made no final decision — while a tug was left partially sinking, another tanker was hit overnight, and an unverified Iranian mine claim muddied the picture further, all days before the US midterm deadline that Gulf states are bracing for.
Sources:
Source: boldvoices.in.

item.title: Saudi/Houthis — Ras Isa port hit, 75-strike claim, fresh airline warning:
item.description:
Houthi-run al-Masirah TV said Sunday that Saudi airstrikes hit Ras Isa port in Hodeidah — a major Red Sea oil terminal — striking a pier and a moored commercial vessel, plus a telecommunications facility southeast of Saada.
Houthi spokesman Yahya Sarea said 75 airstrikes and missile attacks had hit eight Yemeni provinces over 24 hours (Saada, Taiz, Amran, Ibb, Dhamar, Lahj, Hodeidah, Al-Jawf) — Houthi figures, not independently verified. The Houthis also warned that Saudi Aramco facilities are within range and advised airlines to avoid Saudi airspace except over Mecca and Medina.
This follows the coalition's Sunday strikes on Houthi resources in Dhamar and Hudaydah and its interception of a missile and a drone toward the southern region, covered in the evening brief. Sources:
Source: stockbiz.vn.

item.title: Israel — Bennett recommends Eisenkot; Arab-party leaders meet Monday:
item.description:
Naftali Bennett has recommended Gadi Eisenkot to form the government, and the Joint List and Ra'am leaders are scheduled to meet Monday for the first time since the election, saying they will "do everything to replace Netanyahu's government."
Likud accused Eisenkot and his partners of breaking promises on cooperating with parties it describes as supporting terrorism. Analyst Amit Segal sketched two leading scenarios: a minority government dependent on United Torah Judaism, Ra'am and the Joint List, or a national unity government with Netanyahu — either path running past the start of 2027.
Herzog's consultations still begin Wednesday, November 4. Source:

item.content:encoded:

item.title: The Oleshky truce ends — honored to the last hour, and now the question is whether the mechanism survives it
item.description:
The six-day local ceasefire around the Russian-held town of Oleshky expired Sunday evening, and Ukraine's ombudsman said afterward that both sides had honored their commitments throughout — the longest local pause since Russia's full-scale invasion began, ending without a reported violation, and with no announced successor.
The details, as reported by Reuters, show a final day spent getting the last people out before the clock ran out. Ukraine's military said it evacuated 167 people on Sunday from threatened areas of southern Kherson region that had been under daily shelling — including 22 children and 21 people with limited mobility — two days after busloads of Oleshky residents reached Ukrainian-controlled territory on Saturday via Crimea, Anapa and Belarus. The ceasefire, brokered with mediation by US first lady Melania Trump and involvement from Pope Leo, was due to expire at midnight Moscow time (2100 GMT). Kherson governor Oleksandr Prokudin urged residents to stay out of the Dnipro "red zones," warning that "the intensity of Russian strikes there remains high, and the threat to life is extremely high."
The two sides' accounts of what the truce means now point in different directions. Kyiv's ombudsman, Dmytro Lubinets, who personally escorted evacuees out of Oleshky, said after the ceasefire ended that "both sides honored their commitments" and that "it is important to maintain this mechanism of cooperation so that we can continue helping people and saving lives" — language aimed at turning a one-off into a repeatable channel, with Lubinets telling CNN he hopes it can serve as inspiration for other cut-off villages facing the same food and medicine shortages. Moscow, for its part, took a narrower view: Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov, quoted by Russian news agencies, said Russia had a positive view of how the Oleshky operation was conducted and of the coordination between the two countries' human rights commissioners — praise for the operation, not a commitment to repeat it. Pope Leo said he hoped the Oleshky cooperation would pave the way for broader peace efforts, and Melania Trump wrote on X that the ceasefire "has provided residents with the freedom to move, access to food, clean water, medicine, plus a renewed sense of dignity."
For ordinary people, the end of the truce is the return of the war to a place that had six quiet days. An estimated 2,000 civilians were in Oleshky when the truce took hold, of a pre-war population of around 24,000; some chose to stay, some went to Russia, and the rest made the long journey out — Saturday's arrivals included people who told CNN they had not had bread for more than a year and had survived on what they grew or found in abandoned apartments. Elsewhere, the war did not pause for the truce's final day: Reuters reports regional governors and emergency services counted one death in a strike in the Sumy region and at least one in Vinnytsia on Sunday, and in Kyiv, DTEK introduced emergency power outages on Sunday as the capital's grid struggled after repeated strikes — the daytime fallout of the overnight barrage covered in the morning brief.
In short: the Oleshky local truce expired Sunday evening having held without violations, with a final 167 people evacuated from shelling-threatened Kherson areas the same day — and with Kyiv pushing to keep the cooperation mechanism alive, Moscow praising only the operation itself, and the people who stayed in Oleshky now back under the threat Prokudin warned about.
Sources:
Source: duke.fm.

item.title: Doha talks enter a third day with no deal — while a Qatari gas carrier is hit despite reported Iranian clearance
item.description:
Indirect talks in Doha between Iranian negotiators and Qatari mediators entered a third day on Sunday with no agreement on reopening the Strait of Hormuz, even as Gulf states brace for what happens if the talks fail — and even as a Qatari LNG carrier was confirmed hit in the Gulf on Friday, reportedly hours after Tehran had cleared its passage.
The details, as reported by Reuters and carried in the Guardian's Sunday coverage, show a proposal narrowing but not closing. Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi described a Qatari-mediated plan under which the strait could reopen within two days once Washington meets Tehran's conditions — down from an earlier seven-day implementation window — with the release of more than $6 billion in Iranian assets, including funds held in Qatar, at the center of the arrangement. Araghchi called a letter from US Vice President JD Vance a "positive step" but said Iran sees "no need to meet with the Americans at this stage," and no settlement has been announced. President Donald Trump said Saturday that negotiations were "going fine" but that Washington was "not in that much of a hurry," and the Guardian reports Gulf officials are "braced for the worst" ahead of Tuesday's US midterm elections, after which the US moratorium on strikes against Iran is set to expire.
The two sides' positions are still far apart on sequencing. Tehran's conditions, as laid out by Araghchi and by Supreme National Security Council secretary Mohsen Rezaei, include lifting sanctions imposed after the collapse of the earlier Islamabad memorandum, reducing US forces in the region, restoring oil waivers, releasing frozen funds, and recognition of an Oman-discussed shipping route — Rezaei has said the strait stays closed and no talks happen unless all seven conditions are met. Washington, by contrast, has not publicly accepted the linkage between sanctions relief and reopening, and US Central Command said Saturday its blockade of Iranian ports had redirected 144 vessels — a pressure campaign Tehran wants lifted first. The Al Mayeda incident sharpens the disagreement over whether any route is actually safe: owner Nakilat confirmed Sunday that its LNG carrier was hit by unidentified objects in the Gulf on Friday evening, with no crew injuries and no environmental damage and the vessel still operational — while Bloomberg, via reporting carried Sunday, said Pakistan had negotiated safe passage for the Pakistan-bound cargo with Iranian officials only hours before the strike. No one has been identified as responsible, and Qatar's Foreign Ministry condemned the attack and opened an investigation.
For ordinary people, the stakes are winter energy and prices. LNG shipments through the strait ran at roughly 30% of pre-war volumes in October, according to reporting Sunday, and the UK Maritime Trade Operations centre has counted 81 projectile strikes in the strait since July 6, with October the heaviest month of the war — the kind of risk that has already pushed war-risk insurance premiums and freight costs sharply higher and left Brent near $117. A Pakistan-bound LNG cargo turning back toward the Gulf after a strike, even with no one hurt, is exactly the disruption that feeds those costs and, for importers like Pakistan, Japan and South Korea, the worry about winter supply.
In short: Doha's third day ended with a two-day reopening timetable on the table but no agreement, Gulf states bracing for failure ahead of Tuesday's US midterms, and a Qatari gas carrier hit despite reported Iranian clearance — a reminder that, deal or no deal, the waterway's safety is still the open question.
Sources:
Source: azernews.az.

item.title: Israel — Eisenkot lays out four coalition conditions; fraud case weakens:
item.description:
Opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot, in a Saturday-night statement reported Sunday, set four conditions for any coalition partner: recognize Israel as a Jewish state and the principles of its independence, recognize Hamas as a terrorist organization that must be destroyed, accept Israel's governing authority over Gaza, and support mandatory military service.
Joint List chairman Yousef Jabareen has declined to describe Hamas as a terrorist organization, and Yisrael Beitenu leader Avigdor Lieberman has rejected joining a government dependent on Arab-party support — with his 7 seats, Eisenkot would fall one seat short if Lieberman votes against alongside Netanyahu's bloc. Separately, AP reported Sunday that police released two of three suspects in the alleged vote-bribery probe, with a judge criticizing the investigation — undercutting the fraud narrative around the Arab parties' record 19 seats.
Herzog's consultations still begin Wednesday, November 4. Sources:
Source: philpostblog.wordpress.com.

item.title: New CVSS 10.0 — LXD/MicroCloud auth bypass (CVE-2026-112816):
item.description:
A flaw in Canonical's LXD and MicroCloud, published October 30, lets an attacker pose as a trusted client on the LXD network API without that client's private key — giving access to the cluster and the VMs it runs.
Fixed in LXD 6.10.1, 5.21.9, 5.0.11 and 4.0.15 and MicroCloud 3.4.1 and 2.1.5; no known exploitation and not on CISA KEV as of November 1. If you run LXD, patch the snaps.
Source:
Source: carthageelectronics.com.

item.title: Hundreds of thousands lose power as Russia and Ukraine trade overnight strikes — while a local truce holds its final day
item.description:
Russian strikes knocked out power for hundreds of thousands of Ukrainian households overnight into Sunday, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said, in a barrage of 433 long-range drones that Ukraine's air force says it largely intercepted — while Ukrainian drones caused what a Russian governor called "significant damage" to an industrial site in the Nizhny Novgorod region, deep inside Russia. The exchange came on the final day of a six-day local ceasefire around the Russian-controlled town of Oleshky, which held even as fighting elsewhere did not let up.
The details, as reported by Reuters, show both sides hitting energy and military targets. Zelenskyy said Russia hit power infrastructure in four Ukrainian regions overnight and accused Moscow of exploiting a shortage of ballistic-missile interceptors, writing on Telegram that "the intensity of the strikes is very high." Ukraine's air force said it shot down 371 of the 433 drones launched since Saturday evening, with dozens still in the air Sunday morning and six separate drone alerts issued in Kyiv since midnight. On the other side, Zelenskyy said Ukraine hit the Kamensky plant in Russia's Rostov region, which he said makes Russian missiles — Moscow did not comment on that claim. In Nizhny Novgorod, Governor Gleb Nikitin said a large overnight drone attack caused "significant damage" to an industrial facility he did not name; the region is home to the NORSI refinery, one of Russia's largest, and the regional government urged motorists to "buy fuel only as needed and avoid panic buying" while it worked to keep gas stations supplied — a warning that points to fuel infrastructure even though officials did not confirm the target. Russia's Defence Ministry said its forces downed 235 Ukrainian drones overnight; Kyiv did not immediately claim the Nizhny Novgorod attack.
The two sides' arguments are the same ones that have stalled every energy-ceasefire effort so far. Ukraine says it supports a full ceasefire on energy targets, including its own battered grid, but that Moscow is unwilling to agree to one. Russia, which on Friday accused Kyiv of resuming refinery strikes and ignoring a request from US President Donald Trump to stop them — Trump has blamed those strikes for raising diesel prices ahead of next week's US midterms — frames the Ukrainian campaign as a driver of global fuel problems: Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said on state TV Sunday that Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries were adding to global fuel-market imbalances and affecting prices, without mentioning the Nizhny Novgorod strike.
For ordinary people, the night's toll is measured in cold homes and fuel queues. Hundreds of thousands of households lost power as winter approaches, on top of the roughly 280,000 left without power on Saturday, and Kyiv residents spent the night under repeated air-raid alerts. In Russia, the fuel warning in Nizhny Novgorod is the kind of signal that turns a distant drone strike into a local worry about whether the pumps stay full. And the Oleshky exception matters too: a local truce that let hundreds of starving residents out of an occupied town held to its final day — proof that limited pauses are possible, and a reminder of what happens to those who stayed if it lapses Sunday evening.
In short: a huge overnight drone exchange left hundreds of thousands of Ukrainians without power and damaged an industrial site in Russia's Nizhny Novgorod region, with both sides blaming each other for keeping the energy war going — while the Oleshky local truce held to its final day, and what happens next for those still there is now the open question.
Sources:
Source: reuters.com.

item.title: Israel's president urges parties to accept the result — as record Arab-party seats look set to hand Eisenkot the first shot at government
item.description:
Israeli President Isaac Herzog urged the country's political leaders on Sunday to accept last Tuesday's election result and "find creative solutions" to avoid yet another vote, as the arithmetic of a hung Knesset points toward opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot getting the first chance to form a government — with the help of the Arab parties, whose record 19 seats have made them kingmakers.
The numbers are stark. Netanyahu's bloc won 53 seats, the main opposition bloc 48, and the Arab parties — the Joint List (11) and Ra'am (8) — a combined 19 in the 120-seat Knesset, their strongest showing ever. According to a senior Joint List official quoted by Walla and carried by the Jerusalem Post, both Arab parties are expected to recommend Eisenkot for prime minister when Herzog begins consultations — which, combined with the opposition's 48, would give him 67 recommendations, well above the threshold for the mandate. Herzog receives the official results from the Central Elections Committee on Wednesday, November 4, and the new Knesset is sworn in on November 10 regardless of where talks stand. Eisenkot would then have 28 days, extendable by 14, to build a coalition.
The arguments on each side show why recommendations are not a government. Joint List MK Ahmad Tibi said Saturday his party wants to help replace Netanyahu's government but does not want to join it — "We want to be part of the fix, part of the hope," he said, while insisting "there will be no change without the Arab parties." The Joint List would also back removing Likud's Amir Ohana as Knesset speaker and setting up a state commission of inquiry into the October 7, 2023 Hamas-led attack. But Eisenkot, Naftali Bennett and Avigdor Liberman have all opposed depending on Arab parties, while Democrats leader Yair Golan favors cooperation — and the Joint List's chairman Yousef Jabareen refused to describe Hamas as a terrorist organization, a condition Eisenkot set for potential partners. Netanyahu's Likud, meanwhile, has alleged vote-buying and Qatari interference; police arrested seven suspects in an investigation, but election officials have rejected claims of systematic fraud and Ra'am leader Mansour Abbas denies wrongdoing. Herzog's warning on Sunday — "The election results are an established fact — they are the reality" — was aimed at that entrenchment.
For ordinary people, the stakes are concrete rather than abstract. Hadash official Reem Hazzan says Arab voters mobilized against government policies, violence in their communities, and conditions in Gaza and the West Bank, and Palestinian analyst Nidal Foqaha cautions that changes in security, finances and protection from settler attacks may matter sooner than any breakthrough on statehood. If talks fail, the fallback is a unity arrangement or another election — with Netanyahu remaining in a caretaker role in the meantime.
In short: Herzog told Israel's parties to accept a hung-Knesset result on Sunday, and the Arab parties' record 19 seats look set to give Eisenkot the first mandate to try to form a government — but with key opposition leaders opposed to relying on Arab support and the Joint List offering backing without joining, the numbers add up more easily than a coalition does.
Sources:
Source: themedialine.org.

item.title: Hormuz/OPEC+ — targets held, tankers still burning, claims still clashing:
item.description:
OPEC+ agreed in principle Sunday to keep December oil output targets unchanged — 30.9 million barrels a day across the seven members at the table (Saudi Arabia, Russia, Iraq, Kuwait, Algeria, Kazakhstan, Oman) — with no official statement yet and a full ministerial meeting set for November 29 to set 2027 quotas; Brent closed Friday at $117.64.
At sea, Oman's Maritime Security Centre said it evacuated 25 crew from the burning Panamanian-flagged crude tanker RITI in the Strait of Hormuz on Friday, while Iran's Revolutionary Guard said four tankers using "unauthorised routes" were halted or caught fire after hitting mines — claims neither Reuters nor AP could independently verify, and which US Central Command disputes, saying the main transit lanes have been cleared and are safe. UKMTO puts shipping through the strait about 70% below pre-war levels.
Iran's supreme leader was also reported Sunday to have ordered an "unrestricted" military response to any new US or Israeli attack — a reported directive, not a confirmed order, and one more reason the Qatari-mediated reopening proposal remains unresolved. Sources:
Source: tradingview.com.

item.title: Google's first AI answer from orbit — a haiku (catch-up, announced October 30):
item.description:
Google's Project Suncatcher prototype satellite ran its open Gemma 4 model on a data-center-class TPU in orbit and beamed back a haiku — "Blue marble below / Data streams in silent grace / Starlight feeds my core" — which Google calls its first "Hello World" for orbital AI compute.
The satellite, launched October 1 with Planet, carries four Trillium TPUs but can run only one at a time for about 20 minutes on roughly 1 kW of solar power; the real tests — heat dissipation in vacuum and radiation — have not started yet, with two interconnected satellites planned for 2027. A research milestone, not a product.
Sources:
Source: notebookcheck.net.

item.title: DeepSeek Super-Agent Open Source: Free, With Caveats — DeepSeek's dsh-superagent-prototype (October 31, MIT):
item.description:
DeepSeek's Harness team published a research prototype of a proactive coding agent for one GitHub repository, built on the open-source DeepSeek Harness framework — a Router assigns requests from GitHub (and optionally Feishu chat) to isolated Worker sessions.
Reports put it at roughly 4,100 stars within a day, but DeepSeek is explicit that this is research code, not production-ready: Worker sessions run commands without approval as the operator's OS user, Harness has had no security audit, and a sandbox-escape flaw (CVE-2026-82533) was fixed only in version 0.1.2-alpha.1 — use current releases only. Follow-up to Saturday's single-source item, now corroborated.
Sources:
Source: coheser.com.

item.title: Binance restores withdrawals in phases after the $6.3B hack:
item.description:
Binance reopened withdrawals Sunday in a phased rollout starting with bitcoin in a 06:00–09:00 UTC window, then ether, USDT, USDC, BNB and others across 15 networks in phase one, warning of temporary delays from traffic volume.
The exchange says it has now replaced about 95% of the stolen assets (up from 90% Saturday), that major-asset balances are 100% backed and verifiable via proof-of-reserves snapshot, and that the full cryptographic proof is due November 3; no date yet for phase two. The FBI has attributed the October 29 attack to North Korea's TraderTraitor group, according to Crypto News, and President Trump said he would discuss the hack with North Korea if its involvement is confirmed.
Sources:
Source: coindesk.com.

item.title: KEV deadlines land today — Cisco and GitLab:
item.description:
Cisco Secure Firewall ASA/FTD CVE-2026-76418 (CVSS 8.6, unauthenticated VPN-login request forces a firewall reload) and GitLab CVE-2026-97229 (CVSS 10.0, unauthenticated RCE via the CI/CD regex compiler) are both due today for US federal agencies — and the patch-now queue for everyone else.
New context on GitLab: Alpine Linux's post-mortem says attackers attempted the flaw against Alpine's own GitLab server, crashed a worker and downloaded its container image, found no repo/package/release tampering, but could not rule out code execution; and on standard-Ruby installs the October 23 Ruby update (3.3.13/3.4.12/4.0.9) is also required, not just the GitLab patch. Ivanti Connect Secure CVE-2026-111357 remains due Monday, November 2.
Sources:
Source: yourcyberbrief.com.

item.title: Zelenskyy and Erdoğan agree to work on a Black Sea grain corridor — while Erdoğan rebukes both sides over attacks on civilian ships
item.description:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan agreed in Istanbul on Saturday to work together on making the Black Sea grain corridor "exist and be effective," in Zelenskyy's words at their joint news conference — the most concrete diplomatic product of a day that also saw Ukraine strike deep inside Russia and Russia keep hitting Ukraine's power grid. Erdoğan used the same press conference to condemn attacks on civilian vessels in the Black Sea as unacceptable "under any circumstances, regardless of who carries them out or what justification is offered," and urged both Russia and Ukraine to "act responsibly."
The details go beyond the corridor itself. According to Xinhua's account of the talks, Zelenskyy said a significant part of the conversation was devoted to Black Sea security and food security, and that the two sides are preparing new joint industrial and economic projects. Turkey also agreed to step up support for Ukraine's battered energy sector, with generators and other power equipment expected to reach Ukraine as early as next week — a direct response to the Russian strikes that left around 280,000 Ukrainian households without power on Saturday. Zelenskyy said the two discussed the trilateral US–Ukraine–Russia talks expected in early November, with Kyiv wanting Europe — and potentially Turkey — involved, and a meeting in Turkey itself raised as a possibility. The visit fell on International Black Sea Day, October 31, and Zelenskyy described it afterward as "important and substantive."
The two sides' arguments frame the same sea very differently. Erdoğan's position, reported by AFP and Reuters, is deliberately even-handed: he disclosed that Ankara has already sent both Moscow and Kyiv a proposal to stop strikes on civilian ships, and neither side has acted on it. He said he hopes to raise the matter with Russia as well, and that an agreement on shipping safety "would also give fresh impetus to efforts to secure lasting peace." Zelenskyy's argument, by contrast, puts the blame squarely on Moscow: he said Russia has steadily worsened Black Sea security since 2014, and that Turkey supports Ukraine's sovereignty and territorial integrity. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio added a third angle on Saturday, saying from the G20 foreign ministers' meeting in Atlanta that Turkey and India had "come to the table with some ideas" about getting grain moving — though no mechanism, timeline or guarantees were announced in Istanbul, and Russia previously rejected a Turkey–India–Egypt scheme under which flagged ships would call at both Ukrainian and Russian ports without being attacked.
For ordinary people, this is about food prices and winter heat as much as diplomacy. Ukraine's farm economy depends on the corridor, and a significant share of the world's wheat and corn supply moves through it; Zelenskyy told Bloomberg on October 23 that since Russian strikes intensified in August, Ukraine's grain export capacity has fallen to 38% of normal, with agricultural companies reportedly losing around $3 billion. The scale of the shipping danger behind Erdoğan's rebuke is stark: shipping data cited by the Financial Times counts more than 570 vessels hit in the Black Sea this year, with 40 seafarers dead. And for Ukrainians facing winter blackouts, the Turkish generators pledged for next week are the most immediate, tangible part of the deal.
In short: Kyiv and Ankara agreed to rebuild an effective grain corridor and Turkey pledged energy equipment for next week, while Erdoğan publicly rebuked both Moscow and Kyiv over attacks on civilian ships — but with no mechanism announced, no Russian response yet, and Ankara's own shipping-safety proposal still unanswered by both sides, the test will be whether ships stop being hit.
Sources:
Source: signalpostnews.com.
item.content:encoded:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan agreed in Istanbul on Saturday to work together on making the Black Sea grain corridor "exist and be effective," in Zelenskyy's words at their joint news conference — the most concrete diplomatic product of a day that also saw Ukraine strike deep inside Russia and Russia keep hitting Ukraine's power grid. Erdoğan used the same press conference to condemn attacks on civilian vessels in the Black Sea as unacceptable "under any circumstances, regardless of who carries them out or what justification is offered," and urged both Russia and Ukraine to "act responsibly."

The details go beyond the corridor itself. According to Xinhua's account of the talks, Zelenskyy said a significant part of the conversation was devoted to Black Sea security and food security, and that the two sides are preparing new joint industrial and economic projects. Turkey also agreed to step up support for Ukraine's battered energy sector, with generators and other power equipment expected to reach Ukraine as early as next week — a direct response to the Russian strikes that left around 280,000 Ukrainian households without power on Saturday. Zelenskyy said the two discussed the trilateral US–Ukraine–Russia talks expected in early November, with Kyiv wanting Europe — and potentially Turkey — involved, and a meeting in Turkey itself raised as a possibility. The visit fell on International Black Sea Day, October 31, and Zelenskyy described it afterward as "important and substantive."

item.title: Houthi barrage hit Saudi cities Saturday evening into Sunday — and Riyadh airport starts flying again
item.description:
A Houthi missile and drone barrage against Saudi Arabia that began Saturday evening ran into Sunday, according to Al Jazeera's reporting, with Saudi air defences intercepting projectiles over several cities and shrapnel falling in the Mecca province area. Saudi Civil Defence said shrapnel from two intercepted ballistic missiles fell in Jeddah, Taif, Rabigh and Wadi Al-Mughammas, while a drone and a ballistic missile were intercepted over Riyadh during the barrage. By midday Sunday, coalition forces had intercepted a cruise missile targeting Khamis Mushait, with warning sirens sounding across Taif and Jazan, and Al Jazeera reports 10 ballistic missiles directed at the southern region were intercepted in total. The figures are still developing and come from coalition and civil-defence statements as reported by Al Jazeera; independent casualty or damage totals were not available at brief time.
The other side of the exchange kept running too. Early Sunday, Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree warned civilians away from Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport — the same airport hit on October 10, killing 13 people and wounding hundreds. Yemen's government-aligned armed forces said they carried out 736 strikes on Houthi positions over the past 24 hours, with 307 people "neutralised" and 68 military vehicles destroyed — government figures that, like Houthi claims throughout this campaign, are unverified by independent sources. On Saturday itself, the coalition had already reported intercepting a hostile drone over the Riyadh region with no casualties, according to coalition spokesman Turki al-Maliki, and Air India extended its cancellation of Saudi flights through November 14.
For travellers, there is one concrete change: Riyadh announced late Saturday that international flights from King Khalid International Airport would resume from Terminal 2 on Sunday, with Terminal 1 designated for domestic flights, after weeks of suspension and disruption. That partial reopening sits uneasily next to Saree's fresh warning to stay away from the airport — the gap between the official reopening and the threat against it is exactly what passengers and airlines now have to judge.
In short: a Saturday-evening Houthi barrage stretched into Sunday with interceptions reported over Riyadh, Mecca province and the south, Yemen's government claims a heavy counter-strike toll, and Riyadh airport partially reopens Sunday even as the Houthis warn people away from it — all still developing, with casualty and damage figures unconfirmed.
Sources:
Source: aljazeeranews-mggx1uo47w.edgeone.app.

item.title: Apple Intelligence is coming to China in December, with Alibaba's Qwen built into Siri:
item.description:
Apple announced October 31 on its China Newsroom that the first Apple Intelligence features for mainland China enter developer-beta testing on November 4, with the public release in iOS 27.3 in December.
The first wave is the familiar first-generation set — Live Translation, Writing Tools, Visual Intelligence, Clean Up in Photos, Genmoji — on iPhone only (iPhone 15 Pro and newer), with Alibaba's Qwen standing in where other countries can call on ChatGPT. The catch: no Siri AI, no Image Playground, and none of the WWDC 2026 next-generation features; Mac and iPad follow only after further approvals.
Two years after the US launch, this is a real expansion — but a deliberately partial one. Source:
Source: skimwire.com.

item.title: Judge throws out Trump's $10-billion-per-claim defamation suit against the Wall Street Journal — permanently
item.description:
A federal judge in Miami on Saturday permanently dismissed President Donald Trump's defamation lawsuit against The Wall Street Journal over its reporting on a birthday letter to Jeffrey Epstein, ending the case in the trial court for good. US District Judge Darrin P. Gayles dismissed the amended complaint with prejudice in a 20-page order, ruling that Trump had failed for a second time to plausibly allege "actual malice" — the standard a public figure must meet to win a defamation case. Because the dismissal is with prejudice, Trump cannot file another amended version in that court; only an appeal to the Eleventh Circuit remains.
The details matter because this was Trump's second attempt. Gayles first dismissed the case in April 2026, ruling the original complaint relied on "formulaic" assertions of malice that came "nowhere close" to the legal standard. The amended complaint, filed May 27, added new details — including an allegation that Rupert Murdoch told Trump "I will handle it" during a phone call about the article — but Gayles was unpersuaded, describing the malice allegations as "conclusory, vague, sometimes inconsistent with the Article," and writing, "As with his first attempt, he has failed." The suit, filed July 18, 2025, a day after the Journal's July 17 report on a bawdy 50th-birthday letter bearing Trump's name in a book compiled for Epstein, named Dow Jones, News Corp, Murdoch, chief executive Robert Thomson and two reporters, seeking at least $10 billion in damages on each of two claims (outlets differ on whether to call the total $10 billion or $20 billion). CNN reports Gayles also rejected Trump's argument that the Journal should have withheld the story after he denied writing the letter, saying such a requirement would violate the First Amendment: "Were that the law, any time a public figure or his team denies an accusation, journalists would be immediately blocked from publishing."
Each side's next move is already sketched. Trump's legal team said he will appeal and "continue to press forward," and a source familiar with his strategy told CBS News an appeal is likely. The Journal's side, meanwhile, avoids discovery entirely — dismissal at the pleading stage means Trump's team never got the internal newsroom communications it would have sought. Press-freedom groups are treating the ruling as a vindication of the actual-malice standard from New York Times v. Sullivan (1964), which Gayles cited; Trump's supporters frame it as one more round in his broader legal campaign against news organisations, which includes a separate $15 billion suit against The New York Times. Whether the defendants pursue legal fees remains open — the order reportedly did not resolve that question.
For ordinary people, the practical effect is narrow but real: it reaffirms how hard it is for any public figure — including a sitting president — to win a defamation case over reporting they dispute, and it closes, at least at trial level, a case that has shadowed the administration's handling of the Epstein files since last summer. The White House maintains the signature on the letter was not Trump's; the Journal has argued the birthday book, produced by Epstein's estate under congressional subpoena, contains the letter exactly as reported.
In short: Judge Gayles threw out Trump's amended WSJ defamation suit with prejudice on Saturday — the second dismissal this year — finding the actual-malice allegations conclusory and vague; Trump says he will appeal to the Eleventh Circuit, and the question of defendants' legal fees is still open.
Sources:
Source: kioncentralcoast.com.

item.title: Ukraine hit Russia's rocket-fuel factory overnight — while Russian strikes left 280,000 households without power
item.description:
Ukraine's long-range campaign moved from refineries to the munitions chain itself overnight. According to Ukraine's General Staff, reported by the Kyiv Independent via Europe Says, Ukrainian attack drones and Neptune cruise missiles hit the Kamensky Combine in Kamensk-Shakhtinsky, in Russia's Rostov region, overnight on October 31. The General Staff says a finished-goods warehouse caught fire and four production workshops were damaged. The plant makes solid rocket propellant for the Uragan, Smerch and Tornado-S multiple-launch rocket systems, as well as other missile and aircraft weapons, and it has been sanctioned by the EU, UK and US for its role in the war. The same night, Ukraine says it also hit four Russian military supply depots in occupied Donetsk, Zaporizhzhia and Luhansk regions.
Russia has not commented on the Kamensky claim itself — Rostov Governor Yuri Slyusar acknowledged an overnight air attack on Kamensk-Shakhtinsky and four other districts but said nothing about the plant — and the Kyiv Independent notes it could not independently verify the military's claims. That caveat matters, but the plant's role is not in dispute: OSINT project Varta, cited by Militarnyi, describes it as one of the largest chemical plants in southern Russia, producing gunpowder, explosives and ammunition components, and it was already hit by a drone strike on August 24. The General Staff's argument is straightforward: hitting solid rocket propellant production reduces Russia's ability to shell Ukrainian towns with multiple-launch rocket systems. Moscow's side of that argument, repeated throughout the war, is that Ukrainian strikes on its industry are attacks on its war economy — and its own overnight claims ran in the other direction, with the Defence Ministry saying it intercepted 433 Ukrainian drones over 19 regions and struck Kyiv's CHP-6 plant, Kharkiv industrial workshops and a cargo ship off Odesa.
The other half of the night was the toll on Ukrainian civilians. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Russian strikes left around 200,000 households in the Dnipro region and more than 80,000 in the Kyiv region without electricity — about 280,000 in total — after hits on a combined heat and power plant in Kyiv, four electrical substations and a gas facility in Dnipropetrovsk, a power plant in Shostka, and railway infrastructure in Dnipro and Kharkiv. Kyiv's mayor had already confirmed three drone strikes on CHP-6 on Friday night, and on Saturday evening a 12-year-old girl was injured in Kyiv's Obolon district when debris from a projectile fell on a shopping centre, according to the Kyiv City Military Administration. Ukraine's General Staff counted 173 engagements on Saturday, heaviest around Kostyantynivka and Pokrovsk. This is the third night in a row of the resumed deep-strike campaign — Novokuibyshevsk on Thursday night, the Bashneft-Novoil refinery in Ufa on Friday night, Kamensky now — and it comes as winter approaches, when power outages stop being an inconvenience and start being a survival issue.
In short: Ukraine says it damaged a key rocket-propellant plant and four supply depots overnight, Russia claims a huge drone interception and its own strikes on Kyiv's power plant, and the confirmed civilian cost is 280,000 households without power plus a child injured in Kyiv — the energy war and the munitions war now running in parallel.
Sources:
Source: europesays.com.

In short: Ukraine says it damaged a key rocket-propellant plant and four supply depots overnight, Russia claims a huge drone interception and its own strikes on Kyiv's power plant, and the confirmed civilian cost is 280,000 households without power plus a child injured in Kyiv — the energy war and the munitions war now running in parallel.

item.title: Iran says Hormuz could reopen in two days — but only on its terms, and Washington hasn't agreed to them
item.description:
The most consequential diplomatic development of the day is also the most conditional. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi told Al Jazeera on Saturday that talks with Qatari mediators have produced a proposal cutting the implementation time for Iran's plan to reopen the Strait of Hormuz to two days — down from a Qatari suggestion of five. But the plan comes with Tehran's full list of conditions attached: lifting sanctions imposed after the Islamabad memorandum, reducing US forces in the region, restoring oil waivers, releasing all of Iran's frozen funds including money held in Qatar, and recognition of the shipping routes Iran discussed with Oman, with other routes closed. Araghchi called a letter from US Vice President JD Vance "a positive step" toward dialogue, then immediately added that Iran sees "no need to meet with the Americans at this stage" and dismissed reports of a meeting as "media speculation."
That directly tempers the other Saturday reporting. The Qatari newspaper Al-Araby Al-Jadeed, cited by The Media Line, reported that an American delegation is expected in Doha after more than 12 hours of Qatari-Iranian talks in Tehran produced preliminary understandings on Iran's nuclear programme, Hormuz navigation and financial incentives, with China and Russia expected as guarantors. A separate draft framework reported by Al Arabiya English goes further, suggesting Iran's highly enriched uranium stockpile could be transferred to a third country or reduced in enrichment, with Hormuz reopening within seven days of an initial understanding. Neither government has publicly confirmed any of this, and an Axios correspondent cited by Iran International said Tehran and Washington have not agreed to resume direct talks. An Iranian delegation is in Doha, but according to the Revolutionary Guards-linked Tasnim agency, it is there to advance talks with Qatar, not to negotiate with US officials.
Meanwhile the strait itself stayed dangerous. UKMTO reported a tanker struck near Iran's Lavan Island on Saturday; Iran's Revolutionary Guards said it hit a mine after using an "unauthorised route." On Friday, UKMTO reported a small boat attaching limpet mines to a tanker, causing an engine-room fire — described by Reuters via CNBC as the first known successful limpet-mine strike in the waterway since the war began in February. And the market has already priced in the risk: Brent's December contract settled Friday at $117.64 a barrel, up 2.4%, its highest since late April, with the January contract at $113.43; WTI settled at $104.12. Brent finished October up 13.6% and WTI up 15.2%. US average regular gas was about $4.18 a gallon on Saturday, according to AAA, cited by US Brief.
For ordinary people, the gap between the two stories is the whole story. A two-day reopening on Iran's terms would ease fuel prices fast; a failed mediation, three days before the US midterms on November 3, leaves the post-election military option that both sides have been warning about squarely on the table. OPEC+ meets online on Sunday, which may add its own signal before markets reopen.
In short: Iran says Hormuz could reopen in two days if the US lifts sanctions, pulls back forces and frees frozen funds — but says there are no plans to meet US officials yet, reports of a Doha breakthrough are unconfirmed by either government, and oil just closed October at its highest since April.
Sources:
Source: themedialine.org.

item.title: The US ordered its non-emergency staff out of Saudi Arabia as Houthi drones kept coming — four intercepted in a day
item.description:
The US Mission to Saudi Arabia disclosed on Friday that it has ordered the departure of non-emergency government employees and their families from Saudi Arabia, an order that took effect on October 23, citing safety risks from Houthi attacks on civilian airports and critical infrastructure that have caused casualties and major travel disruptions. US government staff must now get special authorisation to use Saudi airports. The embassy noted Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport has partially reopened, while Jeddah and Dammam remain operational with some delays and cancellations. The order is the clearest public US signal yet of how seriously Washington takes the Houthi campaign — even as the US has held off its own strikes since the May 2025 ceasefire.
The attacks behind it continued through Saturday. The Saudi-led coalition said it intercepted four Houthi drones over Medina, Riyadh, and southern and eastern Saudi Arabia on October 30–31, according to coalition spokesperson Turki al Maliki, reported by ISW. The Houthis denied on October 30 that they targeted Medina and have not claimed responsibility for these drone attacks. On the ground in Yemen, government-aligned forces repelled Houthi advances along the Taiz–Aden road in Lahij on October 30–31 with Saudi close air support, and recaptured high ground overlooking al Hazm in Jawf. A separate investigation by Geneva firm AURORAH Geosignal Intelligence, reported by Europe Says, claims Russian satellites were observed over Saudi military and energy targets before and after Houthi strikes — a single-source claim worth noting, not yet corroborated, and it does not change the immediate picture for travellers: airports disrupted, an evacuation order in force, and no sign the drone campaign is slowing.
In short: Washington has formally pulled its non-essential people out of Saudi Arabia, the coalition says it downed four Houthi drones in a day, and fighting inside Yemen is heating up along the Taiz–Aden road — while a claim of Russian satellite help for Houthi targeting remains unverified.
Sources:
Source: cumhuriyetdaily.com.

item.title: AiSOC — open-source SOC with AI agents, v20.4.0:
item.description:
AiSOC is a self-hosted Security Operations Center under the MIT licence: it collects logs, correlates them into incidents and hands them to AI agents that record every prompt and tool call.
Started May 2026, it counts 5,489 stars and 561 forks as of October 31, with v20.4.0 out that day. Worth a look for a home lab or small SOC; note there is no independent security audit on record, and the version number has raced from 8.1.0 in September to 20.4.0, which says more about release pace than maturity.
Source:
Source: pasqualepillitteri.it.

item.title: Binance says 90% of the $6.3B theft is replaced; withdrawals targeted for Sunday:
item.description:
Binance says it has replenished 90% of the cryptocurrency stolen on Thursday (up from ~80%), with its top 10 user assets — BTC, ETH, USDT, BNB, SOL, USDC, XRP, USD1, RLUSD and ZEC — now fully backed at 100%, funded from corporate treasury, its futures insurance fund and a partial SAFU deployment expected within 24 hours.
Withdrawals, paused since the hack, are on track to reopen in phases on Sunday, November 1, subject to security checks. A new proof-of-reserves snapshot (balances at midnight UTC October 31) shows 100%+ coverage for those tokens, but the full cryptographic proof users can independently verify is not due until November 3 — so Sunday's reopening comes before outside verification.
Sources:
Source: Www.coindesk.com.

item.title: Oracle E-Business Suite flaw now seeing exploitation attempts:
item.description:
CVE-2026-101767 (CVSS 9.8) lets someone with no login run SQL as the main APPS database user and then run commands on the server.
Oracle fixed it in its October 20 Critical Patch Update; a week later, decoy servers started catching attackers trying it, and Shadowserver counts more than 670 internet-facing EBS instances. If you run EBS, this is the patch — it is not yet in CISA's KEV catalog as of October 31.
Source:
Source: carthageelectronics.com.

item.title: China-linked Vapor Panda used an open-source AI pentest tool against 200+ organisations:
item.description:
CrowdStrike reports that the state-backed group Vapor Panda used the ARTEX agentic AI penetration-testing framework (paired mainly with DeepSeek and a second commercial model) to target more than 200 organisations across at least 14 countries since October 17, with about 140 showing compromise or moderate-confidence intrusion evidence in 11 days.
Victims include foreign ministries, a European presidency and prime minister's office, defence/intelligence agencies, 19 US organisations in pharma, semiconductors, defence, nuclear and finance, and telecoms in the US, Belgium and the Philippines. The campaign is still active — and it is a case study in why an open-source offensive tool cuts both ways.
Source:
Source: cyberrecaps.com.

The tampered package was not built or published by Anthropic — an attacker gained access to publish it under the legitimate extension identity. If you installed or updated Claude Code in Cursor around October 29, verify your extension version.

item.title: The energy war escalated on both sides overnight — Kyiv lost power and water, a giant Russian refinery complex caught fire
item.description:
Russia and Ukraine traded energy strikes overnight, and both sides' claims point to a sharp escalation rather than a one-off exchange. According to a daily war brief compiling Ukrainian official statements, Russian forces struck Kyiv's critical infrastructure with drones overnight, hitting a facility three times and cutting electricity and water to multiple districts; Kyiv mayor Vitali Klitschko confirmed a critical infrastructure facility was hit, with outages reported in Troyeshchyna, Obolon, Pechersk and several other districts, and parts of the city also left without water. Kharkiv took Shahed-type drone hits across three districts, injuring three people and damaging ten residential buildings, according to mayor Ihor Terekhov. Ukraine's Air Force said Russia launched 134 drones, including 72 jet-powered Shahed models, hitting a combined heat and power plant in Kyiv, four electrical substations and a gas facility in Dnipropetrovsk, and another power plant in Shostka, with railway infrastructure damaged in Dnipro and Kharkiv.
Russia's Defence Ministry, for its part, said its air defences intercepted 433 Ukrainian drones overnight over 19 Russian regions, and claimed its own drone strikes hit Kyiv's CHP-6 power plant, workshops in Kharkiv's Proton industrial zone, and a cargo ship off Odesa. Moscow describes CHP-6 as supplying electricity to military logistics and weapons storage; Kyiv has consistently said Russian strikes on its energy system target civilian infrastructure ahead of winter, and Ukrainian officials had not publicly confirmed the specific Russian claims at the time of writing. Neither side's battlefield figures can be independently verified, and both regularly publish claims the other disputes — but the Kyiv outages are confirmed by the city's own mayor, which is the part that matters for people on the ground.
The other half of the night played out deep inside Russia. The Bashneft-Novoil oil refinery in Ufa, central Russia, caught fire Saturday after a reported Ukrainian drone attack, according to Russian outlet ASTRA, citing open-source analysis of eyewitness photos. ASTRA's analyst said a key catalytic reforming unit, the L-35 — which produces reformate, a high-octane gasoline component, and hydrogen needed to refine motor fuels — was likely burning. Residents reported several explosions Saturday morning, a column of smoke, and internet disruptions after an overnight drone alert, and Telegram channel Exilenova+ reported fires at two of the three refineries in Ufa's northern industrial zone. Bashneft's three adjacent Ufa refineries form one of Russia's largest refining complexes, with a combined capacity of 23.5 million tons of crude a year; Ukraine's General Staff said it hit the same L-35 unit in August 2025.
This is the second night of the resumed refinery campaign, not the first. Ukraine struck the Novokuibyshevsk refinery in the Samara region early Friday, ending a roughly two-week pause that followed heavy pressure from the Trump administration, and Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak confirmed Friday that three oil refineries and one gas-chemical complex were attacked overnight, with two men killed in Samara. Novak warned the strikes "could certainly lead to a reduction in supply volumes" under the diesel deal struck with President Donald Trump, which saw Russia ship about 510,000 tons of diesel in October. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told reporters Tuesday that Ukrainian forces "do not have an order" not to hit refineries, and European allies had advised Kyiv to wait until after the US midterms — advice Kyiv now appears to have set aside.
For ordinary people, the two directions of this exchange land differently. In Kyiv, it is another winter morning of no power and no water in several districts, with private energy provider DTEK saying the capital was suffering electricity shortages again on Saturday after Friday's strikes on energy infrastructure. In Russia, a hit on a catalytic reforming unit at one of the country's biggest refining complexes is the kind of damage that can tighten domestic gasoline and diesel supply — which is exactly why the diesel deal with Washington is now in tension with the refinery campaign. The US-brokered energy ceasefire that briefly held in mid-October is now firmly in the past: Zelenskyy declared that pause over on October 15, and both sides have been hitting energy targets since.
In short: overnight brought confirmed power and water outages across Kyiv districts and a fire at the Bashneft-Novoil refinery in Ufa, the second night of Ukraine's resumed refinery strikes — and with Moscow warning the strikes threaten the diesel volumes promised under its deal with Trump, the energy war is now running directly against the diplomacy meant to contain it.
Sources:
Source: app.osnt.in.

President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told reporters Tuesday that Ukrainian forces "do not have an order" not to hit refineries, and European allies had advised Kyiv to wait until after the US midterms — advice Kyiv now appears to have set aside.

For ordinary people, the two directions of this exchange land differently. In Kyiv, it is another winter morning of no power and no water in several districts, with private energy provider DTEK saying the capital was suffering electricity shortages again on Saturday after Friday's strikes on energy infrastructure. In Russia, a hit on a catalytic reforming unit at one of the country's biggest refining complexes is the kind of damage that can tighten domestic gasoline and diesel supply — which is exactly why the diesel deal with Washington is now in tension with the refinery campaign. The US-brokered energy ceasefire that briefly held in mid-October is now firmly in the past: Zelenskyy declared that pause over on October 15, and both sides have been hitting energy targets since.

In short: overnight brought confirmed power and water outages across Kyiv districts and a fire at the Bashneft-Novoil refinery in Ufa, the second night of Ukraine's resumed refinery strikes — and with Moscow warning the strikes threaten the diesel volumes promised under its deal with Trump, the energy war is now running directly against the diplomacy meant to contain it.
